item.title: NFL news, live updates: Colts release Daniel Jones, Anthony Richardson Sr. to start at QB; Puka Nacua potentially out for season after knee surgery
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news heading into Week 11.
item.content:encoded:
We are officially halfway done with the 2026 NFL season, and the NFL is now into Week 11, highlighted by the year's final international game: the Minnesota Vikings take on the San Francisco 49ers in Mexico City, Mexico, for "Sunday Night Football."

The Indianapolis Colts and Houston Texans opened up the week on "Thursday Night Football," but quarterback Daniel Jones continued to struggle, completing just 44.4% of pass attempts for 144 yards and a pick. The Colts followed up with a statement move on Friday, announcing the team would release Jones and promote former No. 4 overall pick Anthony Richardson Sr. to the starting position in a stunning move.

Los Angeles Rams receiver Puka Nacua might be done for the year after undergoing surgery on his MCL on Tuesday. Nacua was already on injured reserve with multiple injuries, but head coach Sean McVay says that he is now poised to miss "a couple months."

That news came one day after Nacua was reportedly suspended three games by the NFL for violating the league's personal conduct policy, as a result of the receiver's series of incidents this offseason; Nacua is serving the suspension while on IR.

item.title: 5 Dolphins to watch at Bills
item.description: In a rebuilding year, the Dolphins can still cause big problems for Buffalo
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills host the Miami Dolphins on Sunday in a game of two franchises headed in completely opposite directions. The 8-1 Bills sit atop the AFC, leading the conference by one game over the Jacksonville Jaguars and Kansas City Chiefs (the Denver Broncos are also 7-2, but they are currently the No. 5 seed in the playoff picture). Miami, on the other hand, is 1-8 and tied for the AFC’s worst record with the Los Angeles Chargers and Tennessee Titans.

On paper, this a game that Buffalo should win running away. However, games are played on the field, not on paper, and Miami has kept plenty of games close this season. Half of Miami’s losses have come in one-possession games, and they’ve held great offenses like the Chiefs and the Detroit Lions under their season scoring average.

If the Bills want to avoid the pitfalls of a textbook “trap game,” they’ll need to lock in and focus on stopping Miami’s key players. Here are five Dolphins to watch in Sunday’s tilt with the Bills.
_____________________________________________________________________________

RB Ollie Gordon

After De’Von Achane went down with a knee injury earlier this season, it was easy to assume that Miami’s run game would suffer mightily. Thanks to Gordon, though, Miami has been able to run fairly well throughout the course of the year. With former Syracuse Orange quarterback Kyle McCord set to make his second career start this week, Miami will want to try to establish the run and maintain possession of the ball to keep their young quarterback out of obvious passing situations. Shutting Gordon down and keeping Miami in continuous second-and-long or third-and-long scenarios will go a long way towards driving the Bills to victory this week. Buffalo has been good against the run, as they are No. 8 in yards allowed on the ground. Gordon averages 4.2 yards per rush. If the Bills can prevent him from breaking big runs, they’ll be in great shape.

WR Malik Washington

Buffalo’s secondary is beaten up, and while the Dolphins don’t boast a great passing attack, they do have some sneaky-good weapons who can beat you if you aren’t careful. Chief among those weapons is Washington, who leads Miami in targets (51), receptions (36), and receiving yards (400). At 5’8” and 192 lbs., he operates out of the slot more often than not, so it will be up to whomever Buffalo plays inside to contain him. Given their injuries in the secondary, that responsibility could fall to Dee Alford, Jordan Hancock, Damar Hamlin, or a combination of multiple defenders, including linebackers. Washington is particularly good after the catch, as 123 of his 400 receiving yards have come as “YAC” gains. If he catches a short pass, that’s fine; what the Bills can’t do is let him slip tackles and pick up big gains after he makes that grab.

DE Chop Robinson

The 2024 first-round pick is on pace for a career year, and good for him. It took Robinson some time to put it together as a pro, but he has five sacks already on the season, which is one shy of the career-high six sacks he notched as a rookie. He also has 13 quarterback hits, which is just one shy of his career-high total from that same 2024 rookie season. Both Spencer Brown and Dion Dawkins are likely to play this week, so Buffalo should finally be back at full strength along the offensive line after playing some different combinations due to injury over the last three weeks. Making sure that Robinson stays out of the offensive backfield needs to be a major focus of the game plan.

LB Jacob Rodriguez

While the Rookie of the Year hype that came with Rodriguez in the season’s early going has faded a bit, what hasn’t faded is the quality of Rodriguez’s play. The rookie out of Texas Tech has looked every bit the part of a long-term starter at middle linebacker for a Miami defense that has played better than the team’s 1-8 record would suggest. Rodriguez was a fan favorite for many Bills-connected folks during the draft process last spring, and his play so far has justified that hype. He has 80 tackles, four tackles for loss, one sack, one interception, and one forced fumble so far this season. Head coach and offensive playcaller Joe Brady needs to try to give the rookie some different looks by using motion to throw off his keys. That should help Buffalo to make him hesitate just enough to wall up some blocking around him. Buffalo is the league’s second-best rushing offense, but the Dolphins allow just 3.9 yards per rush thanks in large part to Rodriguez’s talent. Neutralizing him in the middle could make for a long day for Miami.

S Michael Taaffe

Taaffe is someone I really liked for Buffalo in April’s draft. He’s a hyper-athletic safety who reminded me a little bit of Cole Bishop. Like Bishop, he’s made some plays here in the early portion of his career, but he’s also been burned for some big gains. Taaffe leads the Dolphins with three interceptions, but he’s also allowed three touchdowns and a passer rating against of 100.7 this season, as opposing quarterbacks have completed 64% of their passes for a whopping 329 yards when he’s the closest man in coverage. If Buffalo can run the ball effectively, that will lead Taaffe to creep closer to the line of scrimmage to help out in run support. When that happens, the play-action pass will be on, and Buffalo could find some big plays through the air. As long as Josh Allen isn’t forcing the ball, he might be able to exploit a young player in Taaffe at the back end of Miami’s defense. If he’s not careful, though, Taaffe is more than capable of turning what looks like a big offensive play into a turnover.

item.title: Question of the Day: How many wins will it take to win the NFC North?
item.description: The NFC North is crazy good. How many wins is it going to take for a team to win the division? You tell us!
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears sit at 7-2, but unfortunately, the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings also sit at 7-2, making it a 3-way tie for first. The Bears currently are losing the tiebreakers to both Detroit and Minnesota, so the Bears technically sit in 3rd place in the division, with the 6-4 Packers in last.

The North is a gauntlet and a half and with 6 divisional games left to be played (4 featuring the Bears), it’s going to be the divisional games that are truly going to decide who is going to win the crown and have home field advantage in the playoffs through at least the first two rounds of the playoffs.

Question of the Day: How many wins will it take to win the North?

I think for the Bears, it’s going to come down to which teams they beat down the stretch. With 8 games to go, however unlikely, if the Bears win their 4 games out of the division and go 1-3 in the games in the division, that’s going to put them at 12 wins, but they will probably not have the tiebreaker against any of the teams in the division if that happens, which means that won’t be enough. But if the Bears go 2-2 outside of the division and 3-1 in the divisional games, that’s also a 12-5 record, but they would be in much better shape in the tiebreaker situation.

Answer. With the 0-2 divisional record, even if the Bears went 3-1 in the division and finished with 12 wins, they probably wouldn’t have the tiebreaker against everyone. If the 1 loss comes to the Packers or Vikings, that team will have the tiebreaker. If Minnesota wins 1 more divisional game, they’ll most likely have the tiebreaker against the Bears. It gets tricky for Chicago and tiebreakers within the division. Unless the Bears go 4-0 in divisional games down the stretch. However, if they do that, with New Orleans and Miami on the schedule, the Bears would be looking at, most likely, at least 6 more wins, giving them 13.

13 is the number. With 3 teams at 7-2, and with how good all four teams are, I just think it’s more likely than not that one of them reaches the 13-win total. I find it hard to believe that two of them will, given they all have divisional games remaining against each other. I think one of these teams finds a way to 13, and that’s the number that wins the North. I think if the Bears or any of the other teams reach 12 wins, that will guarantee them a wild-card playoff spot. If any of them only get to 11 wins, I think that leaves them vulnerable to missing the playoffs. An 11-6 team missing the playoffs would be wild, but if the last-place team in the North finishes 11-6, and the Seahawks or Rams can get to 11-6, that means one of them is going to be sitting home in January with 11 wins but missing the playoffs.

What do you say, Bears fans? Do you think they need to win 13 games to win the division, or do you think a smaller number can get it done? Or do they need to reach an even bigger total?

item.title: Could Bill Croskey-Merritt be Washington’s needed offensive weapon against the Bengals? - Daily Slop
item.description: With Rachaad White nursing a heel injury, Washington could potentially get a timely boost from Bill Croskey-Merritt against Cincinnati's 20th-ranked run defense

The Daily Slop – 21 November 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Commanders Roundtable

Bengals vs Commanders: 3 key matchups to watch

The Jayden Daniels Factor

Number 5 is getting better every week, and last Thursday night at MetLife he proved it in the most important moment of the season so far. The game-winning touchdown drive in the final minutes was vintage Daniels — poised under pressure, decisive, and clutch when Washington needed him most. His PFF overall grade sits ninth among all 33 qualified quarterbacks in the league, and per PFF, the Daniels-to-Antonio Williams connection carries the second-highest passer rating pairing in the NFL. That’s not a coincidence; it’s a reflection of the route-running and timing chemistry those two have built week over week.

The case to force him more targets Monday night is real. Against a Bengals defense that is at its best when it can tee off on a one-dimensional offense, David Blough needs to open the full playbook. That means rolling Daniels out, letting him threaten the edge, exploiting his clean-pocket advantage — PFF ranks him second among all quarterbacks when given a clean pocket — and creating the kind of open-space plays that make the Bengals’ pass rush irrelevant.

Monday Night Football on a national stage with playoff hopes on the line. This is the kind of game Jayden Daniels has been building toward all season. Blough needs to trust him, give him room to operate, and let 5 be 5. The talent is there. The moment is here.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Hogs Haven

The surprising key to victory over the Bengals

Where does WAS have a competitive advantage? Believe it or not, the rushing attack. The Bengals are a poor rushing team, averaging 85 yards per game (30th), while Washington averages 117 (13th). And, for all the gnashing of teeth about the state of the offensive line and the running back stable, Washington is in the top 3rd of the league in rushing yards per attempt (4.3, tied for 11th with the Colts and Jonathan Taylor), while the Bengals are 23rd with 3.9 yards/attempt. Moreover, as I showed in the previous post, rushing defense is the key weakness of the Bengals: they currently rank 20th in rush yards against but 11th on passing yards against. Why play into their hands by getting into a passing showdown when the rushing attack is there for the taking?

Remember that Washington abandoned its zone-heavy rushing attack last week in favor of duo (double team blocking on the IOL) and gap, the approaches used in the prior two years.  That kind of attack recognizes the limitation of Paul at LG and their Centers as zone players and takes advantage of what they do best.  (The other three linemen are zone versatile.)  Well, guess what?  Rachaad White is a star in duo and gap. 

In zone, which Washington has emphasized most of the year, White’s average yards per attempt is 3.93 and his success rate is 35% – far below average numbers in the NFL.  But when he plays duo, he averages an elite 5.27 YPA and has a success rate of 55%.  And when he plays gap, his YPA is an excellent 4.77 and his success rate is 54%. (Data in this paragraph are from Sumer Sports.). It looks like deemphasizing zone and focusing on duo and gap blocking not only fits the OL better, those schemes far better fit their leading rusher. 

If I’m the OC, I plan on running White at least 18-20 times, almost all in gap and duo.  That could give him alone over 100 yards rushing.  Doing so will make the play action game work far more effectively, will protect Daniels, will keep the game close, and will set up the kind of passes that can win a close game.

Washington Post (paywall)

Cincinnati is contending again after recent struggles; can Jayden Daniels & Washington do the same?

The Cincinnati Bengals nearly pulled it off. After the 2021 season, they made an improbable run to the Super Bowl before ultimately falling four points shy of upsetting the Los Angeles Rams. It was only quarterback Joe Burrow’s sophomore NFL season, which fed plenty of optimism about what they could accomplish before his big second contract hit the books.

That hope wasn’t shaken when they fell to the eventual Super Bowl champion Kansas City Chiefs in the playoffs a year later. Cincinnati was viewed as a perennial contender that had plenty of financial flexibility to maximize its window.

The Bengals haven’t made the postseason since.

It wasn’t until this year that Cincinnati (7-2) would be regarded as a serious challenger again. The Washington Commanders (3-5-1) want to keep turning their season around when the teams meet Monday night at Northwest Stadium. The Commanders are rightfully focused on the present, not the big picture. That said, their opponent could provide some valuable long-term lessons.

When assessing the Burrow-era Bengals’ winding path back to prominence, a road map emerges for the Jayden Daniels-era Commanders to do the same.

[T]hat will probably require another offseason retooling. The question is whether the tandem of General Manager Adam Peters and Quinn will be handling that. Owner Josh Harris hasn’t made any public decisions, but it’s worth looking ahead, anyway.

3 Commanders Playing Their Way to a Contract Extension

K’Lavon Chaisson

Through nine starts this season, Chaisson has recorded 24 tackles, 3.5 sacks, and three forced fumbles (already a career high). What he means to the defense was on full display against the Eagles, with a sack and three quarterback hits, but his ability to create turnovers has been his best asset on a team that stressed that exact thing all offseason and in training camp.

Chaisson, 27, played 48 of Washington’s 65 defensive snaps (74%) against the Giants. During free agency this past offseason, he signed a one-year deal worth $11 million with $10.3 million guaranteed and will be an unrestricted free agent in 2027. What Chaisson brings to the Commanders’ defensive edge rotation is more than worth a reasonable two- to three-year extension.

Practice notes | Croskey-Merritt says goal is to play vs. Bengals

Jacory Croskey-Merritt, who has been on Injured Reserve with a groin injury since Oct. 19, had his 21-day window opened earlier this week with the hope that he can return in time for the Commanders’ Monday Night Football matchup with the Cincinnati Bengals. Head coach Dan Quinn was not definitive on whether that would be the case, but Croskey-Merritt was a full participant in Thursday’s practice.

He leads the team in carries, despite missing the last five games, and is tied with Daniels for the most rushing touchdowns. He still leads all Commanders players in rushing yards per game and is third on the team in first downs generated.

Most of the excitement surrounding Croskey-Merritt comes from what he accomplished as a rookie, when he led the team with 805 rushing yards and eight rushing touchdowns. He had two games of at least 95 rushing yards in the final four games of the 2025 season, including a 105-yard day against the Dallas Cowboys on Christmas that featured a 72-yard sprint to the end zone.

Croskey-Merritt’s production this season, however, has been mixed. When asked if he had been dealing with injuries since August, Croskey-Merritt said “it wasn’t the best, but it’s definitely getting better now.” Croskey-Merritt added that a lingering groin issue can affect “anything that you wanna do.”

The goal, Croskey-Merritt said, is for him to be a part of the Commanders’ game plan on Monday. As for whether that will actually happen, he’s taking the “wait and see” approach.

Commanders’ Red Zone Problem Starts Before They Reach the 20

Washington needs more scoring chances against Cincinnati, which has allowed touchdowns on just 40% of opponents’ red-zone trips

The Commanders have 22 red zone possessions in nine games and have converted 12 into touchdowns (54.5%), which ranks 20th in the league through Week 10. According to Sharp Football Analysis, just 29.1% of Washington’s drives reach the red zone or produce a touchdown before getting there, a stat that ranks them 27th in the league.

On the flip side, the Bengals have allowed touchdowns on 12 of 30 red zone possessions (40%), the third-lowest rate in the NFL. The remaining possessions produced 11 field goals and seven scoreless trips.

Jayden Daniels Could Lose Two More Weapons Before Bengals Game

  • Treylon Burks’ nagging foot injury reared its ugly head again Friday as the Washington Commanders receiver missed practice after being a full participant on Thursday. The receiver position is thin with Terry McLaurin, Dyami Brown and Jaylin Lane on injured reserve, so this could be huge heading into Monday night’s matchup with Cincinnati and Joe Burrow.
  • Seeing Rachaad White’s name pop up on the injury report Friday as limited with a heel injury was certainly concerning. Now Washington has to make decisions on two running backs this weekend.

The other backfield concern, Jacory “Bill” Croskey-Merritt, practiced fully for a second straight day as he ramps up in his return from injured reserve. They’ve had mixed success — against the Giants in Week 10, they gave up a 66-yard touchdown pass but also recorded a sack, forced a fumble and intercepted a pass. But Burrow has been fantastic against the blitz, completing his past 21 passes. He also has a 95.2 quarterback rating in his past five games facing extra pressure. “They’ve been good against everything,” coach Dan Quinn said. “Disguise will be big in this game due to, when you go, when don’t you, how do you send it? It’s scheme, but certainly it’s him being able to manipulate it quickly. That’s a big part.” — John Keim

Do you want the Eagles to lose?

I look at the game on Sunday against the Steelers and I think “I hope they lose and improve their odds of getting a higher draft pick.” This will be the first game this year I’ve had that mindset. Actually, this is the first time in many, many years that I’ve had the thought that “it is better if they lose than if they win.” Last week I was hoping Joe Milton would find lightning in a bottle and spark the offense and somehow impossibly be the light at the end of the tunnel that this season might be turned around or at a minimum that the offense would at least have a pulse. More recently, I have been studying the records of the worst teams and checking where the Eagles will draft. I rooted for the Chargers to win over Ravens last week. My “football mind” is upside down now. I’m rooting for bad teams to win and for the Eagles to lose.

The Athletic (paywall)

Colts waive QB Daniel Jones in puzzling cap move, turn to Anthony Richardson in Week 12

The Indianapolis Colts waived quarterback Daniel Jones, the team announced Friday, one day after he finished with no touchdowns, one interception and 144 yards while completing just 12 of 27 passes in a blowout loss to the Houston Texans.

Jones, 29, has struggled all season, throwing 13 interceptions to just seven touchdowns in 11 games while completing a career-low 58.4 percent of his passes. The Colts (3-8) have lost six of their past seven games. Their decision to cut Jones now will result in a $35.2 million dead cap hit for the 2027 season — a figure that could have been significantly reduced had the Colts simply benched him and waited to cut him in March.

Indianapolis signed him to a two-year, $88 million extension in March.

It was the largest two-year extension in NFL history. Nearly $49.5 million of that was guaranteed, and the Colts got some of the league’s worst quarterback play from it.

Jones has $10.5 million in injury guarantees for 2027. So by cutting him, the Colts avoid a potential injury this season that triggers those guarantees. But they also could have just benched Jones for the rest of the year.

Anthony Richardson Sr., the No. 4 pick in the 2023 NFL Draft and once the franchise quarterback, will start the Colts’ Week 12 game against the New York Giants on Nov. 29. Steichen said 2025 sixth-round pick Riley Leonard could also play. He’s the team’s only quarterback under contract next year.

[Because he was released after the trade deadline] Jones is subject to waivers, and teams have until Monday afternoon to place a claim on Jones, who has about $2 million in salary remaining this season. If no team claims him, he becomes a free agent and can sign anywhere.

From The Athletic:

What’s next for Daniel Jones? Sources across the league have varying opinions. Because he was released after the trade deadline, he is subject to waivers, and a team can claim him by 4 p.m. ET Monday.

Sources pointed immediately to the Patriots as a potential landing spot. He and Maye are friends from the Charlotte area, and he could be an upgrade over Tommy DeVito.

Two sources pointed to Arizona, where the Cardinals have traded away Jacoby Brissett and lost Gardner Minshew for the year with a UCL injury. In Tampa, Baker Mayfield is playing through a foot injury with the NFC South always within grasp.

But not only does a team need the $6.25 million in cap space this year, but it must also be willing to take on the risk of $10.51 million being guaranteed next year if Jones gets injured. That represents less than 3 percent of next year’s salary cap, but is still significant for any team taking a flyer on a quarterback who hasn’t played well.

If no one puts in a claim for Jones, he becomes a free agent, which is what happened two years ago after his release from New York. That’s when he signed to the Vikings practice squad. He also could wait after going unclaimed and see how the NFL quarterback landscape shakes out over the next several days.

To read more of this article from The Athletic, CLICK HERE

ESPN

Patriots QB Drake Maye has fractured fibula, may be done for the season

[T]he Patriots are in a rare situation because they have been ravaged by injuries across the roster this season, and are already close to the limit of how many players they can designate for return from IR.

Teams are allowed to designate up to eight players to return from IR in the regular season and then receive an additional two to return from IR in the playoffs. The Patriots have already used five return designations and appear to have earmarked two more for starting left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) and No. 2 receiver Romeo Doubs (scapula), who are eligible to return next week.

So that would leave just one remaining return designation in the regular season, and with others on IR — such as speedy No. 2 running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness) — the team will have to strategize how it manages its roster in that regard.

The Athletic (paywall)

What I’m Hearing on Puka Nacua’s suspension

Here’s what I can tell you about the sort of suspension: The league determined Nacua violated the league’s personal conduct policy, which is a broad policy that serves as a catch-all for what most Westerners would describe as bad behavior. You don’t need a criminal conviction to be suspended, and the NFL doesn’t have to specify what exact rules were broken when handing down a suspension.

But in a letter sent to Nacua this week, the contents of which were reviewed by The Athletic, the NFL said it found “that you bit the woman without invitation or consent.” The “actual or threatened physical violence” against another person, along with “assault and/or battery,” are violations of the policy.

Nacua has not been criminally charged for the incident but, according to the letter, “in lieu of filing criminal charges, L.A. city attorney’s office referred the matter” to a diversion program. Nacua accepted those conditions and is currently completing the diversion program “to avoid the filing of criminal charges.” Essentially, the league’s finding of a violation is based largely on Nacua agreeing to be placed in that diversion program.

The alleged incident took place on New Year’s Eve, and the league was made aware of it around March, according to a source. The NFL opened an investigation, which included reviewing civil pleadings, text messages and other relevant documents. The league interviewed Nacua in October, I’m told; such an interview is typically done at the end of an investigation.

On Nov. 8, Nacua injured his knee. The Rams knew he would miss time but did not know how long he would be out. It is not always cut and dried on how to proceed with such an injury — some warrant surgery while others heal on their own. Nacua sought multiple opinions, and several advised surgery.

I don’t know exactly how many games the NFL wanted to suspend Nacua for, but it was more than three. That desire was communicated to the NFL Players Association and Nacua before the Rams placed him on injured reserve. When the NFL interviewed Nacua in October, it could not have predicted he would go on injured reserve in November. And some within the Rams organization believed last week, before Nacua had surgery, that the suspension was imminent.

Clearly, the timing works in Nacua’s favor, even if he misses the rest of the season and perhaps the postseason. This suspension, like many others over the years, was reached via settlement among the league, the NFLPA, Nacua and his representation. Nacua accepted the league’s three-game punishment — which could be more accurately described as a three-game check forfeiture — and the league walked away with what it considers a precedent-setting victory, even if it’s not viewed that way on the outside.

“Puka would have fought harder had he not been hurt,” one high-ranking official with a team said. “IR gave everybody an out.”

The league will receive blowback from what seems like a flimsy suspension, but it also sets an important precedent for future cases of bad behavior — especially regarding allegations from women who are not domestic partners — that do not involve criminal charges.

Nacua clearly recognized that he would eventually be suspended, and he took the opportunity to serve it while on the mend. If he kept fighting, it could have dragged into the latter part of the season when the Rams try to make the Super Bowl. If he successfully fought to delay the punishment until next year, it would likely come after either a franchise tag or mega extension, when the financial hit would be far more painful.

item.title: Antonio Brown critical of Steelers WR DK Metcalf amidst struggles
item.description: Antonio Brown shared some advice with DK Metcalf amidst his drop issues.
item.content:encoded:
It’s no secret at this point that DK Metcalf has been a massive disappointment ever since he was traded to the Pittsburgh Steelers. His second season in Pittsburgh has been just as disastrous as the first, as he is second in the NFL in drops with 6, while leading all receivers in penalties.

Metcalf leads the Steelers in yards with 432, but has hauled in just 35 of his 71 targets through nine games this season. The receiver admitted to the media that this was the first time he’s dealt with these kinds of struggles in his career, but a former Steeler had advice for Metcalf.

Appearing on “The Matchup” podcast with former Steelers teammate Emmanuel Sanders and Chris Harris Jr., former Steelers standout wide receiver Antonio Brown told Metcalf he simply needs to come back to the ball more.

“I see DK Metcalf trying to box a guy out,” Brown said. “Yo bro, you gotta go back to the ball. Take your nose to the ball. I feel like guys gotta be more confident taking their nose to the ball. You gotta take your nose to the ball first, and your eyes gotta catch it. It’s eyes, nose, hands. Most of these guys, they just use hands, no eyes. You gotta have the concentration. You gotta be focused to be a good pass catcher.”

This sounds like shockingly decent advice coming from Brown, who has gained a reputation for being an internet troll at best over the course of the last few seasons. The concentration quote makes a lot of sense given the sheer number of drops Metcalf has had this season.

Simply put, something has to give with Metcalf. Perhaps with the return of Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson to the Steelers’ offense, things will look smoother for Metcalf and the offense as a whole. Expect Aaron Rodgers to continue to rely on Metcalf down the stretch as the Steelers sit firmly in the playoff picture.

item.title: College football draft targets for the Cowboys: Week 12
item.description: Who are your favorite draft prospects right now?
item.content:encoded:
We’re looking ahead to see who may be on the Dallas Cowboys’ draft card in 2027.

Georgia vs. South Carolina

Georgia enters Williams-Brice Stadium as the nation’s top-ranked team, but South Carolina has enough speed to make this a useful scouting assignment. The Bulldogs’ front will test LaNorris Sellers and the Gamecocks’ offensive line. On the other side, South Carolina has a corner and return specialist whose athletic ability should be apparent whenever the ball comes his way.

Georgia: Gabe Harris Jr., defensive end 

Gabe Harris Jr. has the type of frame NFL teams are always willing to develop. He has the length and mass to play as a traditional defensive end or stand-up outside linebacker. He is not a small speed rusher who has to win before an offensive tackle touches him. He can take contact and hold his ground.

His best work starts with his hands. Harris can lock out an offensive tackle and control the outside shoulder. Against the run, that lets him set a firm edge and forces the ball back toward Georgia’s pursuit. He also has enough strength to squeeze a gap when a tight end tries to block him down. There is useful position flexibility here because Georgia can move him inside on passing downs and ask him to attack a guard.

Why The Cowboys Care

Dallas needs young defensive ends who can survive on early downs. The roster needs another player who can set an edge without coming off the field whenever the opponent gets heavy. Harris would give the Cowboys a power complement in the rotation. He can align outside a tackle in an even front, play the strong side against a tight end and reduce inside in selected passing packages. That versatility would help Dallas keep its fronts less predictable. 

South Carolina: Vicari Swain, cornerback

Vicari Swain is one of the more entertaining cornerbacks in this class because his athleticism appears in two phases. He’s listed at 6-foot and 193 pounds, and he brings genuine speed and excellent open-field instincts. Those traits help him in coverage, but they have also made him one of the country’s most dangerous punt returners.

Swain is comfortable when he can play with vision on the quarterback. He closes quickly from off coverage and has the acceleration to recover when a receiver creates early separation. His movement skills also fit man coverage. He can mirror releases and carry vertical routes.

Why The Cowboys Care

Swain fits the most important item on Dallas’ shopping list. Joey Porter Jr. is the best Dallas has at corner and he’s no guarantee for next season. Swain has the feet to compete outside and the quickness to receive work in the slot, giving the Cowboys options as the rest of the secondary changes around him.

His return value could help him dress immediately. A rookie corner selected outside the first round may begin as the fourth defensive back, but Swain can justify a game-day place through punts and coverage units while competing for defensive snaps. Dallas would gain an explosive special-teams player rather than waiting for a developmental corner to become useful.

LSU vs. Tennessee 

Tennessee is trying to stay in the playoff race after grinding out a road win at Texas A&M. LSU has slipped out of the AP Top 25 at 6-4, but its roster still gives evaluators plenty to study. This matchup puts one of the SEC’s quickest cornerbacks against Tennessee’s vertical passing game and one of the nation’s busiest running backs against LSU’s defensive front.

LSU: P.J. Woodland, cornerback

P.J. Woodland is built differently from Swain. He’s smaller at 5-foot-11 and 164 pounds, so there is no hiding the concern about his frame. What keeps him in the draft conversation is the quality of his coverage movement and his confidence playing the football.

Woodland is at his best in man coverage. His feet are quick at the line and he changes direction without wasted steps. He also has enough recovery speed to remain connected when a receiver threatens vertically. LSU trusts him on an island because he rarely panics when the ball is in the air. He tracks it and competes at the catch point despite giving away weight.

Why The Cowboys Care

Dallas needs coverage talent, and Woodland’s tape supplies it. His quick feet and man-cover ability could translate to the Cowboys’ sub-packages, especially when the defense wants to pressure and cannot afford a corner losing immediately at the line.

Tennessee: DeSean Bishop, running back

DeSean Bishop has gone from a walk-on with one major college offer to the center of Tennessee’s offense. The redshirt junior is a compact runner and his game is built around vision, balance and decisive cuts rather than rare size or track speed.

Bishop presses the line with patience. He allows blocks to form and gets vertical without extra movement. His low center of gravity helps him absorb glancing contact, while his footwork lets him redirect when the initial lane disappears. He is particularly effective on inside and split-zone concepts because he understands how to manipulate a linebacker before making his cut.

Why The Cowboys Care

Javonte Williams can remain the lead back next season, but Dallas should keep adding inexpensive talent behind him. Bishop profiles as a complementary runner who can handle a series or take on a larger workload if the starter misses time.

His running style should fit the Cowboys’ interior concepts. Bishop reads blocks cleanly and gets north quickly. That reliability would make him a sensible Day 3 selection, where Dallas can address the position without spending the premium capital needed at corner, tackle or edge.

item.title: ESPN needs to remove Troy Aikman before Super Bowl: Former Marlins president
item.description: End the awkwardness now.
item.content:encoded:
End the awkwardness now.

Former Marlins president and current Meadowlark sports personality David Samson believes ESPN needs to move on from Troy Aikman now amid his uncomfortable tension with Joe Buck in his contract standoff to prevent a potential disaster when ESPN hosts its first Super Bowl in February.

“Apparently Troy Aikman has gotten to the ‘I don’t give an eff stage’ of his career with ESPN because he keeps doing these things. And here’s the problem — Jimmy Pitaro has to end this,” Samson said Friday on his “Nothing Personal with David Samson” podcast. “I don’t know whether he ends it today, tomorrow, next week or next month, but ESPN cannot have Joe Buck and Troy Aikman call the Super Bowl. They have invested too much money to have any distraction that they know about entering into the leadup to the Super Bowl.

“There’s always going to be something that happens. But if I am Jimmy Pitaro, I am making sure that I find someone to call the Super Bowl right now and that I start the process. So that the audience, that the media, that the gossipers, that we get it all out of our system. We deal with the fact that Aikman is gone from ‘Monday Night Football,’ and we deal with it now. By the time the playoffs and the Super Bowl comes, it’s no longer part of the conversation.”

This ESPN drama centers on how Buck is safe with the network after receiving a six-year, $108 million extension, while Aikman is playing out his contract without a new deal.

Buck and Aikman had an on-field riff before a Bills-Rams “Monday Night Football” game in October that has led to Aikman speaking publicly about his uncertain future.

The former Cowboys quarterback appeared to turn up the intensity by saying on a radio appearance earlier this week: “Well, I know Joe’s always wanted a one-man booth…”

The situation has gotten so awkward that ESPN chair Jimmy Pitaro had to address it.

“Are we happy about the media coverage recently? Of course not,” Pitaro said Tuesday. “It’s been disappointing, but these guys are professionals, and they’re delivering every week. If you watched it (Monday) night, last night was another super high-quality production and telecast. I fully expect that to continue through the season and through the Super Bowl.”

Samson said ESPN boss Jimmy Pitaro has “two children who don’t like each other” and added that viewers don’t like watching two partners who did not get along.

He said Pitaro should at least reach out to Aikman about being professional through the end of the season, which concludes with ESPN hosting Super Bowl 2027.

There are no indications yet that Aikman’s role for the Big Game is in jeopardy, although some have wondered — like Samson — if that could change if this feud continues to fester.

“Because if Jimmy Pitaro does not make a move, and it’s Troy Aikman calling the Super Bowl with Joe Buck,” Samson continued, “what do you think is the first thing that’s going to get talked about? ‘Wow, it looks like in the second quarter there right before the commercial that they looked at each other like a bunch of hated men.’ No, nobody wants that, certainly not ESPN or Disney.

“Wait to see … Troy Aikman will not call the Super Bowl.”

item.description: The Panthers have a lot to prove before fans trust them to live up to their potential
item.content:encoded:
The Carolina Panthers have been on an odd run of injuries, poor discipline, horrible officiating, and good opponents for too long now. Injury luck, if only for the moment, seems to be a tide turning in the Panthers’ favor; discipline may yet prove to be the deciding factor in head coach Dave Canales’ tenure; and the quality of their opponent this week is certainly up for debate. Whether we’re talking Lamar Jackson or Marlon Humphrey, the Baltimore Ravens are perhaps the first team missing as much talent as the Panthers—if not more—that Carolina has seen on their schedule this season.

Enter Jacoby Brissett. The spry, 33-year old, ten year veteran was acquired by the Ravens via trade on November 6th after Jackson and backup quarterback Tyler Huntley were both lost for the season after only five pass attempts against the Buffalo Bills in Week 8. Brissett started his first game just last Monday, November 16th, for the Ravens and attempted 49 passes in a three-point loss to the Los Angeles Chargers.

We don’t know what we’re going to see from Brissett tomorrow. He’s with a new team, has a history of ups and downs as a starter, and is coming off of a short week of preparation. Brissett and the Ravens are a true wildcard. Maybe Will Lee III and Mike Jackson returning will be enough to iron out any concerns over what Brissett and Ravens team in disarray will bring to the field. Then again, we’re pinning a lot of hope there on a rookie corner returning from injury who has shown both promise and a penchant for his own discipline related penalties. That’s not to mention the broader penalty issues or quarterback Bryce Young’s returning lack of consistency. Maybe that’s why, at -2.5, the Panthers are favored over the Ravens in what is tied as the second narrowest spread on FanDuel this week. There are as many reasons to be optimistic about the Panthers in this and future weeks as there are reasons to keep them firmly in the “I’ll believe it when I see it” category.

item.title: Broncos vs. Raiders: 3 Players to Watch in Week 11
item.description: These three players for the Denver Broncos need to perform at a high level to defeat the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
This Sunday, the Denver Broncos take on the Las Vegas Raiders in a classic AFC West rivalry matchup. With an extra week of preparation, the Broncos had plenty of time to figure out a winning gameplan. In order to earn their eighth win of the season, these players need to execute at a high level.

Bo Nix — Quarterback

All eyes will be on Bo Nix this Sunday. Nix hasn’t experienced the uptick in production Broncos Country expected in his third season. Through nine games, he is completing just 61-percent of his passes [a career low], thrown for just 1,730 yards, 11 touchdowns and 4 interceptions. Coming off an ankle injury, he hasn’t been as productive as a runner, though has added 116 yards and two touchdowns on the ground.

Over the past three games, the former first-round pick has played better than he started the season. In that timeframe, he has six total touchdowns and only one turnover. Things appear to be going in the right direction, and I remain optimistic he can turn it up in the second half of the season.

On Sunday, Nix will face Raiders’ defense that is allowing nearly 250 passing yards a game—a bottom 10 mark in the NFL. With that in mind, I’m hopeful to see more production from the third-year signal caller. Nix has just one game this year over 250 yards passing—his Week 2 effort versus the Jaguars.

With extra time to gameplan, I am confident he and the offense will be able to take advantage and put together one of their best performances of the season. I think Nix sizzles in his first game after the bye and starts the second half of the season on a high note.

Riley Moss — Cornerback

Earlier in the week, the Broncos rewarded cornerback Riley Moss with a four-year contract extension worth $67 million dollars. The fourth-year pro has been a key starter in Vance Joseph’s defense the past two and a half seasons.

It’s no easy task playing opposite of All-Pro Patrick Surtain II. For the most part, Moss has passed that assignment with flying colors. The former Iowa standout has a knack for defending passes but has just three interceptions in his career. I’d like to see him start taking the ball away more.

Sunday’s matchup provides that opportunity. The Raiders will be starting Fernando Mendoza. Last weekend against the Seahawks, he struggled but was relatively safe with the football. I’m hopeful Denver’s defensive front seven can get after Mendoza early and often and force him into some bad decisions.

I don’t expect the 2026 NFL Draft’s top pick to test Surtain much at all. That means Moss should be in store for a high-volume day target-wise. Can he rise to the occasion and make a big splash play in his first game after his extension? We are fixing to find out.

Jaylen Waddle — Wide Receiver

When the Broncos traded for Jaylen Waddle this offseason, fans across Broncos Country were confident he would propel their passing attack to the next level. Count me in as one of them. Unfortunately, Waddle hasn’t had that type of impact yet.

His Week 2 performance against the Jacksonville Jaguars sticks out. However, he hasn’t had over 50 receiving yards in any other contest thus far. Through nine games, the former 2021 first-round pick is sporting career lows across the board. In order for Denver’s offense to take flight in the second half of the season, Waddle has to perform much better.

The Raiders have been opportunistic on defense creating turnovers. That’s what they’re good at. Otherwise, they sport a bottom 10 pass defense. Las Vegas has given up the most passing touchdowns of any defense with 22 on the season. They are also allowing the most yards per reception of any team in the NFL.

Opposing quarterbacks have the best rating in the NFL going up against their secondary. With that in mind, this Sunday seems like a prime matchup for Waddle (and the aforementioned Nix) to have a strong connection and create some splash plays down the field.

item.title: Miami Dolphins offensive line review: Tracking the guards in Week 10
item.description: A weekly scorecard tracking the development of Dolphin guards Kadyn Proctor and Jonah Savaiinaea.
item.content:encoded:
When you lose a close game to a bad opponent and your quarterback gets strip-sacked for a defensive touchdown, you might assume the offensive line had a terrible afternoon. The reality is more complicated. The Dolphins nearly completed a 14-point comeback but ultimately fell 24-22 to the Colts in Week 10, a game that highlighted a seemingly downward trend for the team as a whole.

That may be especially true for the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea remain key pieces of the Dolphins’ future. While the offense struggled as a whole, player development doesn’t stop because of one ugly afternoon, and that’s especially true for two young guards expected to be part of the foundation moving forward. Each week, we take a closer look at Proctor and Savaiinaea and examine what analysts are saying about their most recent performances.

Kadyn Proctor

Jonah Savaiinaea

What We Learned

When you think of the ideal offensive line, you’re probably thinking of five guys who have played together for a long time and who understand what the quarterback likes to do in certain game situations. At this moment in time, the Dolphins have none of that. In Week 5, Savaiinaea misses most of the game due to injury. Proctor misses Week 8 while in concussion protocol. Against the Colts, Andrew Meyer played the entire game at center while Aaron Brewer is treated for his own concussion, and the team is led by a brand new quarterback in Kyle McCord. With all of these injuries and new faces, you can’t really be surprised when plays break down and players don’t know where to go.

A big reason why the offensive line held up as well as it did – even without Brewer – is Kadyn Proctor. There’s an old line about offensive linemen: Strong o-line performance slips by the average viewer – it’s when you make a mistake that you stand out. Proctor has been steady most of the season, but especially lately: Fewer bad reps as the season moves along, with steady, consistent growth. His PFF grades averages out to a slightly above league-average 61.9, which is remarkable for a rookie, and his pass protection over the past two games is bordering on elite. LockedOn Dolphins’ Kyle Crabbs said this week that Proctor’s last three games “have graded as the three best games that he has played this season.”

As for Jonah Savaiinaea, the picture is a little murkier. Crabbs has been increasingly critical of his play since the bye week, arguing in the same video that the Colts game featured several examples of the inconsistency that plagued him as a rookie. One missed block late in the game potentially cost Ollie Gordon a significant gain during Miami’s final drive. That said, PFF ranked his performance against the Colts as his second-best overall and against the pass. Maybe Savaiinaea is just slow to develop (remember how long it took Austin Jackson to turn into a serviceable starter?), and the last month has raised questions about how much of Savaiinaea’s hot start was sustainable. Jonah for sure has more development to do, especially against the pass (PFF grades <45 in 3 of the past 4 games). I still have hope.

One last point we touched on before: Perhaps more than anywhere else on the team, offensive line performance is a team effort, especially as opposing defenses become more nuanced and creative. Offensive-line play is often evaluated as if the five linemen operate in isolation. They don’t. A failed run can be traced to a guard losing a block, but it can also be caused by a tight end missing an assignment (cough Dulcich cough), a receiver failing to seal the edge, a protection call that never gets communicated or the absence of an All-Pro center who normally keeps everything organized. Against Indianapolis, we saw examples of all of the above.

That’s why a strip-sack, a stuffed run or a pressure allowed doesn’t always tell the full story. When looking at o-line scoring, I try to remember that context matters.

The tracker will be updated each week throughout the season. For a more in-depth breakdown of Proctor’s and Savaiinaea’s performance, check out offensive line Coach Eric Smith’s film analysis of the game, which you can find on his YouTube channel, Focused on Fins.

item.title: Previewing the New York Jets’ opposition: Los Angeles Chargers
item.description: The Jets are on the road to take on the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
The last time the Jets beat the Chargers, they were still representing San Diego and Plaxico Burress scored three touchdowns. Since that time, New York have lost five straight times to them, including a 27-6 drubbing in their most recent meeting in 2023.

Let’s break down the Chargers’ roster going position by position:

Quarterbacks

Justin Herbert was a pro bowler last season, but he’s having a rough year in 2026, with career-worst numbers in almost every category. In his first six seasons, he averaged 27 touchdown passes and 11 interceptions per year. However, over halfway through the 2026 season, he has thrown for just six touchdown passes and already has 11 interceptions.

He didn’t have a very productive game as a passer against the Ravens on Monday night, but at least he managed not to throw an interception for the first time all year as the Chargers finally won their first game to improve to 1-8. He also rushed for a season-high 51 yards and a touchdown.

DJ Uiagalelei is the backup but he’s completed just two NFL passes in his career.

Offensive Line

Incredibly, five of the Chargers’ eight active offensive linemen are rookies, although this is hardly by design. They have five offensive linemen on injured reserve, including well known names like Rashawn Slater, Tyler Biadasz, Trevor Penning and Trey Pipkins. Pipkins was activated for practice last week, though, so his return is possible on Sunday. His official game status is questionable.

Unsurprisingly, this has led to the Chargers struggling to protect Herbert, who has been sacked 33 times. Only Deshaun Watson has been sacked more often that that this season.

The only two players to start every game so far have been second round rookie Jake Slaughter at center and veteran right guard Cole Strange.

At the moment, Joe Alt is at left tackle, with sixth round rookie Logan Taylor at left guard. Slater and Penning had started off the year on the left side, but Alt moved across from right tackle and Taylor stepped in when each of them got hurt. Since Alt’s move, fourth round rookie Travis Burke has been starting at right tackle.

Alt has a team-high seven penalties and Strange, who has also given up a team-high three sacks, has six.

The three players currently on the bench are veteran guard Kayode Awosika, sixth round tackle Alex Harkey and the undrafted center Jacob Spomer. Awosika and Harkey have started two games each this season.

Running Backs

Los Angeles’ top running back, Omarion Hampton, last season’s number one pick, is still averaging less than four yards per carry behind the banged-up line, although the Chargers rank 10th in the NFL for rushing offense. He’s coming off his first 100-yard rushing performance of the season in the win over the Ravens.

Keaton Mitchell and Kimani Vidal both get work as backups to Hampton but they combined for just four yards on five carries in the Ravens win. They have caught 30 passes and scored three touchdowns between them, though.

Scott Matlock is also on the roster as a fullback with Alec Ingold on injured reserve.

Pass catchers

The leading receiver so far this year for the Chargers is last year’s second round pick Tre Harris who has 26 catches for 348 yards but no touchdowns.

You would have expected Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnson to produce more alongside Harris but they’ve only started eight games between them and combined for just 31 catches. However, they’ve flashed big play potential with Johnson averaging 19 yards per catch and McConkey averaging 17. On Monday, McConkey – who is questionable for Sunday – was inactive and Harris was the only Charger with more than 16 receiving yards.

At tight end, Oronde Gadsen II has caught 20 passes and Charlie Kolar has caught 15, but David Njoku has been a non-factor. Njoku could play more this week, though, because Kolar has been dealing with a concussion and is listed as questionable.

The backups at wide receiver are Theo Wease Jr., KeAndre Lambert-Smith, Derius Davis and fourth round rookie Brenen Thompson. They’ve combined for 12 catches, half of which were by Lambert-Smith. Thompson is listed as doubtful for Sunday.

Defensive Line

The Chargers operate with a 3-4 system that employs Jamaree Caldwell, Dalvin Tomlinson and Teair Tart as starters. They are poor against the pass, but middle of the pack against the run, and held the Ravens to 16 yards on 15 carries on Monday night.

Fifth round rookie Nick Barrett and Justin Eboigbe are the backups inside. All five have played at least 140 snaps with Tomlinson having contributed 2.5 sacks.

Linebackers

The Chargers drafted Akheem Mesidor in the first round but he’s currently coming off the bench behind veteran Khalil Mack and 2025 pro bowler Tuli Tuipolotu. While none of the three has more than three sacks, they’ve combined for 8.5. Mack leads the team with six tackles for loss, while Tuipolotu leads them with 16 quarterback hits.

At inside linebacker, Daiyan Henley plays a full-time role and wears the headset. He leads the team with 62 tackles but has been bothered by a knee issue all year, which even nixed a potential trade to Denver. The knee issue has ruled him out for Sunday.

The other starter has been former Jet Del’Shawn Phillips, although Henley was sometimes the only off-ball linebacker on the field. Backups Troy Dye and Marlowe Wax don’t get to play much but Wax should have a bigger role with Henley out.

Bud Dupree and Caleb Murphy are the backups on the outside but neither has played much.

Defensive Backs

Aside from all their injuries on the offensive line, the Chargers have also been deeply impacted by pro bowl safety Derwin James being on injured reserve.

Tony Jefferson and Elijah Molden are the current starters at safety, although RJ Mickens and fourth round rookie Genesis Smith have also played over 200 snaps each.

Kendall Williamson is also on the roster but hasn’t played on defense and has been listed as out anyway.

Tarheeb Still and Donte Jackson are the starting cornerbacks with Still reverting to the slot in nickel packages and Cam Hart entering the game on the outside. Hart has two interceptions and a team-high eight pass breakups.

Still practiced all week but showed up on the injury report on Friday and is listed as questionable.

Backups Rodney Shelley, Isas Waxter and Deane Leonard have all played less than 100 snaps at cornerback. Shelley is another undrafted rookie but he’s been ruled out, while Waxter is also listed as questionable.

Special Teams

The Chargers’ kicking game is pretty solid with kicker Cameron Dicker having only missed two kicks all season. He also has the third-lowest opponents’ kickoff return average in the NFL. While punter JK Scott’s raw numbers are not eye-popping, Pro Football Focus currently ranks him first in the league based on their grades.

Davis, Mitchell and Vidal have all seen work on kickoff returns, with nobody managing a 35-yard return so far this year. The Jets should be wary of Davis, though, as he had an 87-yard punt return for a touchdown against them in 2023. He’s averaging 10 yards per return on punts with Thompson and McConkey listed as his backups.

Jets fans may recall what a good special teams contributor Phillips was, and he’s continued in that vein by leading the Chargers in special teams tackles again despite moving into the starting unit. He led the entire NFL last year.

Wax, Murphy and Dye are also productive, while the primary gunners have been Lambert-Smith and the backup cornerbacks.

item.title: Saints vs. Bears: Key Matchups
item.description: After falling to 3-6, the Saints need to utilize these key matchups to comeout with a win on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints are walking into Chicago as double-digit underdogs against the Bears. The Saints have dropped two of their last three, and their season has quickly been derailed.

Now in desperate need of a win, New Orleans will face their former head coach and current Bears defensive coordinator, Dennis Allen, in a game they were completely outmatched in just a year ago. If the Saints want to steal a win, it will be by taking advantage of these key matchups.

QB Tyler Shough vs. Bears pass rush

Saints fans will be the first ones to tell you about Allen’s capabilities as a defensive playcaller. The former Saints head coach was known for his ability to call up exotic looks at the line of scrimmage, something that has become even more relevant this season with the massive success of Brian Flores and the Minnesota Vikings defense.

Tyler Shough has been a bright spot for the Saints this season, but is coming off one of the more disappointing games of his career. Even worse for Shough and the Saints, this was against a lackluster Carolina Panthers defense. Now New Orleans will be facing a team that is top-10 in sacks and just made a massive trade for one of the best defensive linemen of the decade, Jeffrey Simmons.

The Saints have worked on getting the ball out faster, and it’s improved over the weeks. But pass protection remains a major concern, and with a switch at center, right guard, and right tackle, the Saints could be in for a long day.

Saints running backs vs. the Bears’ run defense

I don’t think I even have to elaborate here. The Saints are a bottom-five rushing offense in the league, and are coming off a game where running backs averaged 1.5 yards per carry against one of the league’s worst run defenses in the league. Now New Orleans will be facing a team that is top-five against the run.

Getting the run started has been a problem all season, and really, it’s more of a Kellen Moore issue than it is a running backs issue. But if the Saints are going to have any chance at keeping up with Chicago’s high-powered offense, it will be by controlling the game on the ground.

Saints pass rush vs. QB Caleb Williams

The Saints have two of the most dangerous pass rushers this season, with Carl Granderson logging 8.5 sacks and Chase Young getting 8 of his own. Fortunately for the Saints, they’ll be facing a quarterback who holds on to the ball the longest in the NFL. Unfortunately for New Orleans, Caleb Williams’ time from getting the ball and releasing it hasn’t translated into sacks.

Over the last two games, Williams has been sacked just twice and has become a playmaker in the face of the pass rush. The former first overall pick’s stats haven’t looked great this season, throwing just 8 touchdowns to 5 interceptions, but he has grown into a leader and can command an offense with the best of them. If the Saints want a chance at winning this game, they’ll likely have to take down the star quarterback three or more times and create impossible goal-to-go situations.

item.title: Cardinals QB issues continue: Beck or Johnson to start?
item.description: Remember in training camp this position had a glute of talent?
item.content:encoded:
During training camp this year, both the quarterback and receiver rooms were overflowing with talent and capable bodies. Now, the pass catchers are backups to backups, while the QB room is down to two rookies and a guy who is being paid by his 17th NFL club.

This weekend as the Arizona Cardinals are preparing to play the Kansas City Chiefs, one of the best teams in the AFC, the coaching staff just might be starting its fourth quarterback this season. Rookie Carson Beck may not start.

RELATED:SHOULD THE CARDINALS MAKE A CLAIM FOR QB DANIEL JONES?

Beck started his first NFL contest last week in the 34-6 beatdown from division foe Los Angeles Rams. He was scheduled to start again this weekend as center Hjalte Froholdt has been released from concussion protocol.

But Beck has had some flare-ups with back spasms. Although the team hasn’t ruled Beck out for the Chiefs game, journeyman Josh Johnson is being prepped to start instead. If Johnson does play, that will become four starting quarterbacks in four games. What a QB turnstile.

Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur stated that the team is taking Beck’s situation one minute at a time, which made it sound serious since he avoided the classic “one day at a time” standard answer. Beck did not participate in practice on Friday while the coaching staff is waiting to see how the young signalcaller responds to treatment. The rookie QB was previously sidelined with back spasms earlier in the season.

LaFleur added:

“We’re not gonna shut the door on him, but we’re gonna proceed as if Josh [Johnson] is gonna be starting on Sunday.”

Beck was taken in Round 3 of this year’s NFL draft and basically was the emergency quarterback for the majority of the year. Then Jacoby Brissett was shipped off, and suddenly Beck was the backup to Gardner Minshew against the Seattle Seahawks. Minshew became injured in that game and then was placed on IR after surgery to repair his () in his throwing arm.

Which meant, the next man up. Beck started against the Rams as the Cardinals offensive line did not provide much protection and sacked Beck five times, which could just as easily been double digit numbers. Beck finished going 11 for 18 for 108 yards and two picks, of which one was the receiver’s fault.

Johnson is 40-years old. He was a fifth-round selection of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers way back in 2008. The Cardinals are his 17th NFL team. He has played for three clubs twice, plus was a roster member of an UFL team, an AAF franchise, and the XFL where he was the passer rating leader. He played in five games for Washington in 2025 with two starts.

Beck was seven years old when Johnson was drafted by Tampa Bay. Johnson has always been the backup, or the backup to the backup. He has played in just 50 NFL games with a mere 11 starts. His total career passing yards is 2,669, what most starters eclipse in a single season. Johnson has a career 58.7% completion ratio with 94 rushing attempts for 481 yards, so he is mobile.

Which means he has experience. If Beck can’t go, rookie Joey Aguilar will become the backup with WR/KR Devin Duvernay the emergency QB.

item.title: 5 Bills to watch vs. Dolphins
item.description: Can the Bills keep their roll going against another AFC East foe?
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills are looking to extend their current winning streak to six games this week as they take on the Miami Dolphins, who are looking to avoid extending their own three-game losing streak. In 17 matchups with No. 17 at the helm against Miami, the Bills are 14-3. While the Dolphins did win the last time these two teams met, scoring a decisive 30-13 victory over Buffalo last November, much has changed since then.

For starters, neither team’s head coach from that game is with the club, as former Buffalo head coach Sean McDermott is unemployed, and former Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel is the offensive coordinator for the 1-8 Los Angeles Chargers. Miami has torn the team down to the studs, as quarterback Tua Tagovailoa, running back De’Von Achane, and wideouts Jaylen Waddle and Tyreek Hill are either no longer with the club or injured. Buffalo, meanwhile, has started the Joe Brady era by winning eight of their new head coach’s first nine games.

How can the Bills avoid dropping what should be a winnable game against a rebuilding divisional foe? It would help if their top players performed well, but with some injuries to navigate, the Bills will have some new faces stepping up this week. Here are five Bills to watch against Miami on Sunday.
_____________________________________________________________________________

QB Josh Allen

Allen has long dominated the Dolphins, posting video-game numbers against Miami for the whole of his career. Allen has completed 66.6% of his passes for 4,608 passing yards, 45 passing touchdowns, and 11 interceptions. On the ground, he’s run for 723 yards and five scores on 101 carries against Miami. Remember, this is across 17 games. Allen traditionally does great things against the Dolphins, and I’d expect that he’ll continue that trend this Sunday. He might not run for the kinds of yards that he did in years’ past against Miami, especially with a game coming up on Thursday night, but he will definitely be a central figure in the action. Look for the Bills to give Allen some quick-hitters early to establish a rhythm before hitting some big throws on play-action as the game progresses.

TE Dawson Knox

Dalton Kincaid is doubtful to play thanks to thumb and ankle injuries, and while it’s entirely possible that he suits up, he’ll likely be limited even if he does play. That means that Knox may have a chance to step up against a Miami defense that has not defended opposing tight ends well this season. George Kittle, Travis Kelce, Mason Taylor, T.J. Hockenson, Mike Gesicki, and others have either had big games or scored plenty of points—in real and fantasy football—against Miami. Knox isn’t elite, but he is a reliable target for Josh Allen as his longest-tenured pass-catcher. If Kincaid is able to go, I expect he’ll break off a big play or two, but if he can’t, expect Knox to have his best day of the season.

OLB Greg Rousseau

Groot is the kind of guy who can just wreck anything the Dolphins have going for them on offense. Against second-year man Kyle McCord, who will be making his second start, Rousseau presents a problem for multiple reasons. First, his length gives him the ability to block passing lanes that would otherwise be open. Second, he is shifty enough and strong enough on the edge to make McCord uncomfortable regardless of the situation. Third, the Dolphins are very weak at tackle, and having someone like Rousseau out there with Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, Bradley Chubb, T.J. Sanders, and T.J. Parker doesn’t bode well for a struggling offensive line. Austin Jackson, Miami’s starter at right tackle, is ranked No. 71 out of 72 qualifying tackles at Pro Football Focus. He’s No. 69 in pass block grade and No. 65 in run block grade. Rousseau should be excited to see Jackson across from him this week.

LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr

The rookie is likely to start this week with veteran Dorian Williams out due to a calf injury he suffered in last week’s win over the New York Jets. That’s a big loss for Buffalo, as Williams has been very good of late. However, the team is high on Elarms-Orr, and he has flashed some big-hitting ability early in his career. He’s appeared on just 21% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps this season, totaling 18 tackles, but he alreayd has two fumble recoveries to his name, as well. He’s struggled a bit in pass coverage, so look for Miami to try to manipulate him through motion and play-action early. Will the Bills call veteran Shaq Thompson up from the practice squad to supplement the linebacker group this week? And, if they do, will Thompson eat into Alarms-Orr’s playing time? We’ll find out on Sunday, but look for No. 52 to make some big hits this week.

CB Maxwell Hairston

The second-year man has looked totally lost this season, as a rookie year that flashed some potential has given way to a second season where he has lost not only a shot at a starting gig, but really any shot at playing many meaningful snaps. Rookie Davison Igbinosun has far outplayed Hairston this season, but with Christian Benford out this week, Hairston has a chance to build back some trust with the coaching staff. Miami’s passing game isn’t exactly elite—it’s not even league-average, as the Dolphins rank No. 31 in attempts, No. 29 in passing yards, and No. 29 in passing touchdowns—so this is a good time for Hairston to make a play or two. I think the ship has sailed, at least for now, where we look at Hairston as someone who should be playing when all of Buffalo’s corners are healthy; however, it would be nice for him to have a week where he looks like someone who could play in a big spot if needed. That’s a low bar to clear, but one he’s consistently knocked over throughout this season. Veteran Tre’Davious White may see time as a practice squad elevation, too. If Hairston can’t see snaps and play effectively this week, then it might be time for a bigger conversation about the former Kentucky product.

item.title: Chiefs-Cardinals: 5 questions with Revenge of the Birds ahead of Week 11
item.description: We welcome Revenge of the Birds for answers to five questions about Arizona before Sunday Afternoon’s Week 11 matchup.
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Arizona Cardinals in the early afternoon slot of Week 11 games. We welcome Seth Cox of Revenge of the Birds— our sister SBNation site covering the Cardinals— for Five Questions with the Enemy.

Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app!

Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time.

  • Chat live throughout the game
  • Browse with fewer ads
  • Easily jump between communities
  • Enjoy faster commenting and posting

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Revenge of the Birds community through Sunday’s game to get perspectives from both sides of the Week 11 matchup!

1.Rookie Carson Beck completed 11 of 18 passes for 108 yards with two interceptions and five sacks in his first NFL start. What would meaningful progress look like for Beck in his second start at Arrowhead?

This may sound insane, but leading a touchdown drive.

Since the miracle win against the Dallas Cowboys, the Arizona Cardinals have not scored a touchdown. They have three field goals.

So, against the third ranked scoring defense, let’s just shoot for a touchdown and improving as a unit as they head into a more realistic schedule from a competitive standpoint after this debacle in Kansas City.

There is also now a chance the Cardinals don’t even start Beck as he is dealing with back spasms.

2. Arizona has traded Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jacoby Brissett while describing the remainder of the season as an evaluation period. What have those decisions revealed about the direction general manager Monti Ossenfort and head coach Mike LaFleur are taking the franchise?

Man, talk about an organization talking out of both sides of their mouth.

The trade for Marv was after a complete dumpster fire to start the season for him, then they moved Brissett because he was benched and wanted out.

Then the cavalcade of injuries has led to Josh Johnson likely starting a game in the year 2026 in the NFL.

You had two veteran quarterbacks that would keep you competitive. You drafted a running back third overall because you needed to get a piece that fit what Mike LaFleur wanted to do on offense; you paid Trey McBride and Michael Wilson super high-end money because this wasn’t a rebuild.

And within 10 weeks, it is not only a clear rebuild, but a complete teardown… except trading a 30-year-old safety on a bottom-three defense in the NFL.

Nothing that has happened makes sense.

3. With Michael Wilson on injured reserve, Trey McBride has become the clear centerpiece of Arizona’s passing game with 78 receptions, 635 yards and five touchdowns. How can the Cardinals prevent Kansas City from taking away Beck’s most reliable target?

McBride was always the focal point, but the injury to Wilson made him the only legitimate target. The Cardinals wide receivers remaining to throw to:

Devin Duvernay – six receptions 57 yards
Simi Fehoko – two receptions 38 yards
Harrison Wallace – one reception nine yards
Reggie Virgil – three receptions 54 yards
Zay Jones – no catches no yards

The Cardinals entire wide receiver room for the season: 12 receptions 158 yards

Those are not the stats for last week, those are for the entire season. 

So, it’ll be a lot of Trey McBride, but the Rams and Seahawks have put the gameplan out on letting him get receptions and not gaining yards. And now it could be Josh Johnson starting… yay!

4. The Cardinals rank 31st in points allowed and surrendered 436 total yards, including 202 rushing yards, against the Rams. What is the biggest weakness in Arizona’s defense that the Chiefs are equipped to exploit?

Being on the field?

They seem to be okay covering, but they are terrible at rushing the passer, and covering for four seconds in the NFL is not ideal. They cannot stop the run, but I genuinely think Emmett Johnson may not be needed as much because the Chiefs will likely be up by so much. 

The Chiefs will be able to throw the ball if they want, run the ball if they want, score as much as they want. It will be a complete cluster on Sunday.

5. What is your prediction for how Sunday’s game unfolds, including the final score?

The Cardinals have not scored a touchdown in two games. I don’t see that changing with Josh Johnson as the quarterback after just 10 days with the team.

Chiefs 31, Cardinals 6

Good luck and good health to the Chiefs in this one.

The Pittsburgh Steelers take on the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday afternoon in an interstate battle. The Steelers are coming off a tough loss on SNF at the hands of the Cincinnati Bengals, and the Eagles have their eyes squarely on draft season. With the AFC North up in the air, Pittsburgh can ill afford to let this winnable game slip through their fingers.

Our friends at FanDuel Sportsbook have the Steelers as 4.5-point favorites on the road in Philadelphia. The over/under is set at 37.5, and the Steelers are moneyline favorites at -205.

Here are three prop bets to target on Sunday.

Germie Bernard – player to record 10+ yard reception: -280

Yes, I get it. Bernard threw up a goose egg on SNF, but hear me out. The Steelers will look to get their passing game back on track altogether, and Philadelphia is a great place to start. Bernard has a total of 57 receiving yards in his last three games after his big game against Tampa Bay. The Eagles allow the ninth-highest EPA per target to slot receivers.

Remember, Bernard will need just one ten-yard catch. You can feel safe with this prop.

T.J. Watt records a sack: +106

Watt was shut out against Cincinnati, but nobody had a good game on Sunday night football. Plus, the Bengals offensive line is much improved. Joe Milton was sacked seven times against the New York Giants. In fact, Philadelphia has allowed 14 sacks over their last three games. Big bounce-back week for the Steelers defensive line, and you can bet Watt will join the party.

Jaylen Warren anytime TD: +130

Warren hasn’t scored since Week 8, and Rico Dowdle has taken more and more snaps from the running back, including last week, in which he out-snapped Warren for the first time this season. The Steelers figure to be playing with a lead and the ability to possess the football makes me believe this streak is snapped on Sunday. The line may say 4.5, but I don’t see how the Steelers don’t win this one wire-to-wire.
