item.title: NY Giants’ pass defense has been much better than expected
item.description: The Giants’ pass defense ihas been among the league’s best.
item.content:encoded:
There were, if not outright concerns, certainly questions about how good the New York Giants defense could be in 2026.

Between edge defenders Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, and Kayvon Thibodeaux, as well as off-ball linebackers Tremaine Edmunds, Arvell Reese, and Micah McFadden, the Giants’ linebacking corps was expected to be one of the best in the NFL. And the hope was that their defensive line would at least be serviceable after the addition of veteran defensive tackles D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris.

The bigger questions were about the Giants’ secondary, particularly after Cor’Dale Flott left in free agency.

2025 free agents Paulson Adebo and Jevon Holland hadn’t panned out in their first years as Giants, while 2023 first round pick Deonte Banks had regressed badly under DC Shane Bowen and was considered a bust. The Giants signed former Cleveland Browns and Jacksonville Jaguars cornerback Greg Newsome II, as well as former Baltimore Ravens safety Ar’Darius Washington, in the 2026 free agency period and drafted Tennessee cornerback Colton Hood in the second round of the draft.

However, those moves weren’t viewed as much more than Band-Aids for a Giants’ secondary, and national commentors suggested that the Giants’ scondary could be putrid in the first year of John Harbaugh’s rebuild.

Fast-forward nine games, and the Giants’ secondary has been much, much, better than anticipated under Dennard Wilson, Donald D’Alesio, and Addison Lynch.

The Giants are currently fielding the NFL’s fourth-best defense in total yardage allowed (2,751 total yards). They’re third-best in passing yardage allowed per game (184.1 yards per game), second in yards per completion allowed (9.8 yards per completion), and 2nd in yards per attempt allowed (6.2 yards per attempt).

The Giants are accomplishing this feat with smothering coverage from their starting corners. Both Deonte Banks and Greg Newsome II have been incredibly sticky in man coverage, allowing little separation for receivers.

Banks is allowing just 2.1 yards of separation as the nearest defender, per NFL NextGenStats, while Newsome is allowing all of 2.6 yards of separation. Banks and Newsome are both forcing tight window throws on over 40 percent of the plays in which they’re the closest defender — which is exactly what the “step coverage” Dennard Wilson’s defense calls for.

(note: “step coverage” calls for the defensive back to be within a step of the offensive player)

And while slot corner Dru Phillips is allowing more separation (3.6 yards on average), he’s allowing -5.9 EPA in coverage and a Catch Rate Over Expected of -13.0 percent.

Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson praised the Giants’ safeties when he spoke to the media on Thursday, saying,

“I think Ar’Darius played his best game the last outing against Washington. Obviously, he tackled extremely well. You saw him, in the fourth quarter in a critical situation, come up with an interception. He’s been doing everything that I know he could do, from being around him in Baltimore when he was there. He is a smaller guy that plays with a big stick. He is going to attack the line of scrimmage. He tackles well. He can cover. So he’s doing a good job. I think all the safeties are doing a good job in their role. It’s kind of safety by committee. All of them deserve the opportunity to play. So that’s why we’ve been playing them.”

And Wilson wasn’t just puffing up his players. Each of the Giants’ safeties have played very well in coverage as well.

Jevon Holland has been among the best safeties in the NFL this year, allowing a -27.8 percent catch rate over expected which is 3rd best among all DBs in the NFL and -13.4 EPA allowed. Jason Pinnock has proven to be remarkably sticky in coverage

The Giants’ airtight coverage is allowing them to lead the NFL in the rate of Cover-0, that is man coverage across the board, at 10.8%. That jumps to 11.8% in obvious passing situations, and the Giants are sixth in EPA allowed in those situations.

Interestingly, the Giants’ pressure rate has been remarkably low when only rushing four defenders, even with their sticky coverage. That’s led to frustrations from fans when it comes to sack totals (or the lack thereof), particularly with regard to Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux. Both of the Giants’ starting EDGEs have elite get-offs, but have all of 2.0 sacks between them.

NextGenStats has shown us that part of the problem is that the Giants’ opponents specifically game plan for their hyper-athletic pass rushers. The Giants’ opponents feature the second-fastest Time To Throw of any defense in the NFL, as well as a Top-3 deviation from their usual Time To Throw.

The Giants’ sticky Cover-0 packages work with Wilson’s aggressive blitz patterns (as he refers to them) to provide an answer.

The Giants are now second only to the Minnesota Vikings — and the madman that is Brian Flores — in the average number of pass rushers sent at 4.90.

The Giants are currently sitting at 5-3-1 on the season, and they can thank their defense for closing out four of those wins, as well as forcing the tie against the Washington Commanders.

All told, the Giants’ secondary has been one of the most surprising units in the entire NFL, and it’s powering a defense that is finally playing up to its potential. I suspect they’d be getting much more attention on the national level it weren’t for the low sack numbers and what Flores is doing in Minnesota.

Now, the Giants will need them to keep it up, or perhaps even find another level if they can.

item.title: Steelers KR Kaden Wetjen could be benched for undrafted free agent
item.description: The Steelers special teams could look quite different in Week 11.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers selected wide receiver Kaden Wetjen in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft out of Iowa. Listing Wetjen as a wide receiver was a bit of a stretch, though, as he was really known for being one of the nation’s most electrifying return specialists during his time with the Hawkeyes.

To this point in his NFL career, Pittsburgh has yet to reap the benefits of selecting the return man in the fourth round. This could explain why one Steelers insider believes that Wetjen could be upended by an undrafted free agent as soon as this weekend.

Appearing on 93.7 The Fan on Friday, Ray Fittipaldo of The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette suggested that the Steelers could replace Wetjen in favor of the highly recommended Max Hurleman.

Fittiplado reported earlier in the week that Rodgers had mentioned that he would like to see Hurleman to get some reps on special teams, a sound explanation for his belief that the undrafted free agent could get a helmet this Sunday.

Many members of the Steelers organization have sung the praises of Hurleman in the past week, including Aaron Rodgers, Mike McCarthy, and DK Metcalf. Earlier in the week, the team opened up Hurleman’s 21-day practice window, clearing the path for him to return from injured reserve.

The receiver had put together two strong training camps with the team but has yet to appear in a game. There seems to be too much smoke to ignore right now. Pittsburgh has plans for Hurleman, and he could get a helmet as early as this week.

Another week without Kenneth Walker III? It's looking that way for the Kansas City Chiefs.

After missing Week 10 due to groin tightness, the Chiefs running back did not practice this week and has been ruled out for Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals. Rookie Emmett Johnson, who rushed for 101 yards and caught two receiving touchdowns last week, will once again take on the starter's role.

On Friday, Reid said Walker, as well as offensive lineman Jaylon Moore and guard Trey Smith, are "improving" as they deal with injuries, but all have been ruled out.

Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua underwent surgery to repair his MCL this week, head coach Sean McVay announced on Friday. The procedure will rule him out for the next few months, which could result in him missing the rest of the 2026 NFL season.

"We always thought [it] was a possibility," McVay said regarding Nacua's surgery. "It's going to be a couple months and we're going to have to go on without him."

The 6-4 Rams, who are on a bye in Week 11 and play Thanksgiving Eve against the Green Bay Packers, are currently tied for second in the NFC West and have seven more games left in the regular season. McVay did not have a definitive timeline for a return. The team is currently scheduled to play its Week 18 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Jan. 3, a game that could be flexed depending on what the playoff picture looks like at the time.

McVay did not rule out a Nacua return should the Rams make the postseason, but said, "you're planning on not having him."

Other Week 11 injuries to monitor:

  • Luther Burden III (concussion) has cleared protocol after taking a helmet-to-helmet hit in Week 8 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The Chicago Bears wide receiver logged three full practices this week and carries no injury designation. Same goes for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, who was limited this week with a knee issue. "Like 99 problems, but this ain't one," he said.

  • Injuries that kept him limited in Wednesday's practice did not keep Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers (ankle/quad) away from being on the field Thursday and Friday. The Raiders' leading receiver exited Sunday's loss to the Seattle Seahawks after just 11 snaps with an ankle issue. He is currently listed as questionable.

  • The Cardinals are preparing to start 40-year-old Josh Johnson against the Chiefs as Carson Beck (beck) sat out Friday's practice. Johnson, who is on his 15th NFL team, would end up being the team's fourth different starter at quarterback in the past four weeks following Beck, Gardner Minshew and Jacoby Brissett.

  • DeVonta Smith (hamstring) has missed the past three games for the Philadelphia Eagles, but says he's 100% and has felt that way for a while. Smith said he was able to play last week against the Carolina Panthers, but some things are out of his control. He carries no injury designation for Week 11.

item.title: With no Rams game, who are you rooting for?
item.description: Take an R&R day, there’s a storm on the horizon
item.content:encoded:
While it has been another gripping week for Los Angeles Rams fans, the Week 11 bye offers both the team and its fans a brief respite until Thanksgiving Eve potboiler. That’s when the Green Bay Packers take to steed from the frozen tundra of the North, marauding west into the City of Angels. How L.A. handles this battle will be the harbinger for a stretch of games, with all games bigger than the previous.

There could be nothing better than the Rams gaining ground in the playoff race while on a day off. There are three games this Sunday that have some meaning to L.A. fans. Get down on the rail and root them home.

Here’s how to follow these three important games.

New Orleans Saints (3-6) @ Chicago Bears (7-2)

Kickoff: 10 a.m. PST

Location: Soldier Field in Chicago, Illinois

Network TV broadcast: FOX

Play-by-play: Kevin Burkhardt

Color analyst: Tom Brady

Sideline reporters: Erin Andrews and Tom Rinaldi

To keep it simple, Rams fans can clearly root against the NFC North every week over the final eight weeks. The Bears, Lions, Packers, and Vikings are all within reach and surmountable. This one’s a long shot. The weather will be rather mild for this time of year, 58 degrees, with morning rain that may linger after kickoff.

A wet track favors Chicago, they lead the NFL in run attempts and rushing yards per game, while New Orleans languishes in the Bottom 10 defending the ground attack. Although two the Saints three wins have come on the road, their offense is plodding, particularly the run game. It won’t help that three starting offensive linemen are out.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) @ Detroit Lions (7-2)

Kickoff: 10 a.m. PST

Location: Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan

Network TV broadcast: FOX

Play-by-play: Kevin Kugler

Color analyst: Daryl Johnston

Sideline reporter: Allison Williams

The Lions are 5-0 at thus far and have already banked victories over division rivals Minnesota and Detroit. They could get caught looking past the Bucs, with their eyes on a big Week 12 home meeting with the Chicago Bears. All six of Tampa Bay’s losses have come by seven points or less.

The Buccaneers have one the top rushing offenses in the league, but rank at the bottom in passing. They like to to make full use of the clock, most seconds per play (2nd), time of possession (3rd), and time of possession percentage (3rd). Detroit has fairly balanced offense (55% pass), but likes the chunk plays, they land fourth in explosive plays.

Minnesota Vikings (7-2) vs San Francisco 49ers (8-1)

Kickoff: 5:20 p.m. PST

Location: Estadio Banorte in Mexico City, Mexico

Network TV broadcast: NBC

Play-by-play: Mike Terico

Color analyst: Cris Collinsworth

Sideline reporter: Melissa Stark

No matter how this game falls, the Rams gain ground on a squad ahead of them. I get it, rooting for the ‘Niners is like a snake eating a porcupine, only once a lifetime and you have to be in dire straits. West coast rivalry aside, the Vikes have a fairly soft schedule after Sunday. It seems prudent to root for them to beat up on San Francisco and then later on their division rivals, Detroit and Chicago.

San Francisco has been an offensive machine so far and trending up, 400 yards or better and 33 points per game over three straight outings. The defense is salty against the run, but is below the midline stopping the pass. Minnesota’s blitzing defense had carried the team and its lack of competent quarterback play. Now that Kirk Cousins is at the throttle, the offense might be able to pull its own weight.

item.title: Cowboys vs. Titans: Offensive, defensive impact players in Week 11
item.description: Which Cowboys do you think could stand out on Sunday?
item.content:encoded:
If there’s such a thing as a cakewalk victory in the NFL, this Week 11 matchup with the Tennessee Titans could be it for the Dallas Cowboys. The Titans currently holds the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, and as such, are considered one of the worst teams in the league. That should equate to an easy “W” for the Cowboys.

Since there’s no such thing as a guaranteed victory in the NFL, the Cowboys still need to remain vigilant this week and do everything within their power to secure their fifth victory of the season. In order to do that they need everyone to play at their best. Some players have a way of impacting the game more than others, which we’ve identified below.

Offense – QB Dak Prescott

Okay, it’s somewhat cheating to pick the starting QB as the offensive impact player this week, but that’s exactly what we’re going to do anyway. Dak Prescott should have a huge game in this Week 11 matchup against the Tennessee Titans. The Titans secondary currently ranks dead last (32nd) in the league in passing yards allowed (266.9) and No. 4 should be able to pick them apart at will.

With the weapons at his disposal, Prescott should be able to slice and dice Tennessee’s secondary. George Pickens could have another big game after last week’s 145-yard, three-touchdown performance and CeeDee Lamb should hit the 1,000-yard receiving mark (currently sitting at 976 yards). Throw in Ryan Flournoy’s clutch catches when needed and Dallas’ aerial attack should be lethal this week.

Defense – DB Caleb Downs

The last two games have been interesting for Caleb Downs, the Cowboys first-round pick this year. He played arguably the best game of his young career in Week 9 against the Indianapolis Colts, but maybe one of his worst last week against the San Francisco 49ers. Experiencing ups and downs for a first-year player is be somewhat expected, but we believe he will bounce back in a big way this week against the Titans.

With Christian Parker losing his playcalling duties we believe No. 13 will be put in better position to play to his strengths in Week 11. Mike Petine will likely have him playing more around line of scrimmage, quite possibly using him as a blitzer more this week than we’ve seen in past weeks. Against a second-year QB and a talent deprived offense, we fully expect Downs to make several impact plays to help secure the “W” for the Cowboys.

item.title: Packers should lean on running back Kaleb Johnson after their bye
item.description: If the ground game is going anywhere, it’ll be because Kaleb Johnson drags it there.
item.content:encoded:
The bright spots of the Packers’ Week 10 loss to the Vikings are few and far between, but running back Kaleb Johnson was surely among them.

“I thought he did a nice job,” LaFleur said of Johnson’s 10-carry, 42-yard outing. “I liked how he was hitting the hole, running with good pad level, pressing the line of scrimmage. I thought that was a positive performance.”

If there’s a big takeaway to be had here, it’s that Johnson should be getting the lion’s share of carries going forward, and probably deserves more snaps, too. 

Josh Jacobs remains a mystery. He’s on track to return in relatively short order from finger surgery, but a potential suspension still looms like the sword of Damocles. He wasn’t overly effective as a runner in his brief return to the lineup, either. Across three games, Jacobs carried 36 times for just 80 yards, an abysmal 2.2 yards per carry. Even the perpetually disappointing MarShawn Lloyd has managed 2.7 yards per attempt this year.

Speaking of Lloyd, even if he’s better than Jacobs this year, he’s obviously not the future or the present at the position. Kudos to him for making it all the way back from his various injury issues over the last couple of seasons, but it’s abundantly clear he can’t get the job done. It’s hard to foresee him improving much even if the Packers make major strides on the offensive line.

Chris Brooks, meanwhile, is a solid but limited player. It’s probably better to think of him as a fullback at this point, a latter day John Kuhn who mostly finds his way to the field because he’s not going to screw it up for the Packers in pass protection.

And since Pierre Strong Jr. has now been released, that leaves us with Johnson as the last remaining back on the roster, and perhaps the most viable.

The big problem with Johnson to this point has been his limited value in the passing game. You can see what the Packers think of him there by just look at his snap usage. He was on the field for 13 snaps against the Vikings and carried the ball on 10 of them. As a rule, they don’t want him catching passes or blocking for Jordan Love.

But LaFleur did call out Johnson’s pass blocking as his most notable contribution on Sunday. Johnson stonewalled a blitzing linebacker on a 19-yard completion.

“The thing I was most pleased with was one of the protections when we hit [Tucker Kraft], he came across and picked up Eric Wilson on the blitz right in the B gap,” LaFleur said.

You don’t have to be a tape grinder to see what LaFleur is talking about. Johnson lines up to Jordan Love’s left on the play, but alertly comes across the formation to pick off Wilson just as he jets past Travis Glover. Love completes the pass to Kraft, and the Packers would go on to score three points on the drive, cutting the Vikings’ lead to just 10 points. In theory, it could have been a pivotal play.

The fact is that Johnson is the only back doing anything even close to making pivotal plays this season. The Packers have only had a back rush for 40 or more yards in a game three times this season, and Johnson is responsible for all three of those occurrences. The Packers will probably never have a good running game this season, but if they’re going to do anything at all on the ground, it’s probably going to be because Johnson is getting the work done.

item.title: Chargers first win comes at a price
item.description: The Los Angeles Chargers may be in the win column, but it isn’t all roses and rainbows.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 1-8 going into their Week 11 matchup against the New York Jets at SoFi Stadium.

The Chargers can breathe a sigh of relief as they won’t go winless, but they have lost the inside path to the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.

In this week’s Reacts poll, 43% of fans said they would be okay if the Chargers didn’t get the No. 1 overall pick.

The Chargers would have the chance to trade out of the pick with a team looking to select a quarterback, or they could take someone like Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith, which could completely change their offense.

In last week’s Reacts poll, the confidence meter to determine whether the team is heading in the right direction, is at 13 percent.

It’s a slight step down from the 14 percent mark the team was at last week, but one win isn’t enough to rebuild all of the confidence zapped from the eight-game losing streak to start the season.

The Chargers are hoping to win their first home game of the year against the Jets at SoFi Stadium. Kickoff is scheduled for Sunday at 1:05 pm PT. Fans can watch the game on CBS or stream it on the Paramount Plus app.

item.title: How To Watch UNC Football battle Virginia
item.description: Here’s how you can watch the Heels as they attempt to secure bowl eligibility against the Cavaliers.
item.content:encoded:
Well, we’ve made it to Thanksgiving week. This weekend always feels a little different because we all see the big holiday on the horizon, and that holiday ushers in a joyous and very hectic time of year.

There hasn’t been a lot to be thankful for with the football team in Chapel Hill. They really don’t havea any bigger things to play for, and unfortunately with their home loss to Louisville this past weekend all that’s left is hoping to have a three game improvement over last year. Which they paid $20 million for.

It’s pretty clear that the powers that decide who will be on TV at particular times have agreed that Carolina fans are checked out on this football team. The amount of blue visible in the stands was one hint, and now we know the last two games of the season will be played at the noon hour on…not exactly the marquis destinations for the ACC.

For the first time this year, the Tar Heels will grace the screen of the CW, and they do so on a weekend that has the best game of the conference being Miami playing Virginia Tech to where they are hosting College GameDay. Truly, it feels like we are just playing out the string.

Still, there’s some interesting stuff to watch for. This week it’s who will be under center as Carolina—rightfully—has been cagy as to whether or not Billy Edwards, Jr is well enough to play or if the Tar Heels will trust Travis Burgess in his first start under Bill Belichick and Bobby Petrino. There’s also Jelani Thurman’s quest to be at the top of a pretty impressive group of Tight Ends at UNC, and Jordan Shipp continuing to enhance his stock for either a NIL payday or hearing his name called on the NFL Draft stage next May.

Then next week at high noon there’s the car crash that is one team literally playing the game before they get taken over by a coach versus the other team that hasn’t beaten them in years to the point where they’ve seen that squad plant the flag in their field. The league was so excited about that matchup it’s at Noon on the ACC Network, so here’s hoping they don’t need a shot down the sideline to help determine a big call.

Either way, there’s some intrigue today as the Tar Heels and Virginia face off. If you aren’t going to be in beautiful Charlottesville today, here’s how you can catch the action:

  • Time: 12:30 PM ET
  • Location: Scott Stadium — Charlottesville, VA
  • TV: The CW with Thom Brennaman handling play-by-play, Jason Cabinda doing color, and Wes Bryant working the sidelines to once again try to get something out of Bill Belichick. Good luck.
  • Radio: Tar Heel Sports Network with Jones Angell doing play-by-play, Joe Jauch with color, and Bryn Renner on the sidelines. Here’s a list of affiliates airing the THSN broadcast. You can also listen to them on GoHeels.com, The Varsity Network, Tune In, and Sirius XM on channel 266.

item.title: Eye of the Tiger: Pivotal position matchups for LSU vs. Tennessee
item.description: Three key matchups for a tough road game in Neyland Stadium
item.content:encoded:
Although the College Football Playoff wishes have sailed for LSU, there’s still very much at stake in this game. Sitting at #9 with an 8-2 record, Tennessee is in a great spot to make the 12-team playoff for the second time under Josh Huepel. Each of their losses were by just a field goal. The first came at the end of September to then #1 Texas, then on the road at South Carolina. They have won 5 of their last 6, which is impressive considering they made a quarterback change 5 weeks ago.

The Volunteers entered 2026 with a massive question mark at the QB position. They felt strongly about last year’s starter, Joey Aguilar, being able to get another year of eligibility, but he didn’t. They then turned their attention to none other than…Sam Leavitt. We know how that story went, though. Lane Kiffin flew to Knoxville to meet Leavitt in the airport and convince him to commit to LSU and the rest is history.

True freshman Faizon Brandon started the first 5 games of the season for Tennessee, but it was never pretty. So, Huepel turned to redshirt freshman George MacIntyre and he’s gone 4-1 as the starter.

LSU heads to Tennessee with a disappointing 6-4 record after a crushing collapse at home against Texas last week. Their season is effectively over and they are playing for pride for these final two regular season games.

We’ll get our first peek at what Lane Kiffin’s coaching looks like when things are going poorly. Will the Tigers come out fired up and looking to play spoiler? Or will they cower and lose their third straight?

We’ll find out starting at 2:30 pm on Saturday in Neyland Stadium and here are three key matchups to look out for:

Sam Leavitt vs. Tennessee defense

This one is pretty broad, but things are at an all time low for Leavitt. He was criticized heavily in the media for leaving the field prior to the alma mater as the team’s leader, there were anti-Leavitt chants by students as they exited the stadium, and when given the ability to clear the air about some of when speaking publicly on Monday, he avoided it.

Now, he heads to Knoxville, the place he left high and dry to come back down to Baton Rouge. The Tennessee defense is ranked 3rd in total defense, 1st in scoring defense, and 1st against the pass. They sack the quarterback as much as anyone in the conference other than LSU, sitting just one short of the Tigers. It’s a tough matchup, in a tough environment, in a tough time for Leavitt.

LSU offensive line vs. Tennessee defensive line

As I just mentioned, the Volunteers can get after the quarterback. They’ve racked up 39 sacks in 10 games. While 7 of those did come from Tyree Weathersby Sr, who is out for the season, they have plenty of other dudes that can get it done.

Xavier Gilliam and Mariyon Dye have 6 and 5 sacks, respectively, on the defensive line. Although he’s listed as a linebacker, Arion Carter can come off of the edge and has 4 sacks of his own.

Sam Leavitt was clearly hobbled last week against Texas. It looked to be his right leg/ankle, which is different from the left hamstring that he was successfully playing through earlier in the season. He looked hesitant to run and became scared to throw the ball after his third interception, putting his offensive line in a tough spot where they had to protect while he scrambled around in the backfield. That led to a few holding penalties when he exited the pocket before they expected him to.

Where this somehow gets even more concerning is when LSU tries to run the ball. As good as Dilin Jones is, he’s had to make a lot of his magic on his own by making defenders miss. With Leavitt potentially compromised and the Tigers being in a hostile environment, they badly need to find a rushing attack to keep the Jim Knowles defense honest.

LSU run defense vs. DeSean Bishop

Blake Baker’s run defense has been excellent all season. Despite missing Whit Weeks since week 4, they’ve been able to limit opposing running backs on a consistent basis. They’ve mostly been able to limit opposing offenses, in general, all season, but even when the other team has been able to move the ball, it’s typically not on the ground. They’re ranked #2 in the SEC in rush defense, allowing just 86.1 yards per game. Opponents are averaging just 2.73 yards per carry.

This week presents a true challenge, though. Allow me to introduce you to DeSean Bishop, the SEC’s leading rusher. Wearing #18 for the Volunteers, Bishop has rushed for 1,163 yards with 13 touchdowns. He’s averaging 5.1 yards per carry and has very seldom been slowed down. The only team that has limited him was Texas, who held him to 34 yards rushing in week 4.

Bishop has surpassed the century mark in rushing yards in 6 out of 10 games this season. In 2 of the games that he didn’t, he finished with 97 yards. The only outliers are that game against Texas and their week 3 game against Kennesaw State, in which he had 9 carries for 42 yards and a touchdown before they took him out of the blowout and let then backup Daune Morris run for 116 yards.

The bottom line is, Tennessee can run the ball. Their offensive line is playing like one of the best in the country. They’ve only thrown the ball for over 200 yards twice the entire season. Brandon did it in the season opener against Furman and MacIntyre did it in his first start at Arkansas. Aside from that, the Volunteers have gotten to 8-2 and #9 in the country by running Bishop and playing defense.

item.title: 5 Things I Think I Think About the Miami Dolphins After Week 10
item.description: The Dolphins lost 24-22. And also just won the 2030 Super Bowl? It's complicated.
item.content:encoded:
If you’re looking for a silver lining after the Miami Dolphins’ 24-22 loss to the Indianapolis Colts, I have good news: The franchise may have found themselves a new hero, and it’s Zane Gonzalez. Here are 5 things I think I think after the head-shaking loss to the Daniel Jones-led Colts.

Zane Gonzalez: Miami Dolphins Superfan From the Future

It’s February 10, 2030. 

At Nashville’s Nissan Stadium, the New York Jets just won their first Super Bowl in more than 50 years. Gang Green is celebrating: Champagne, laughter, tears. Three years earlier, the Colts had traded away the pick that became the No. 1 selection in the 2027 draft. Now the quarterback chosen with that pick has delivered New York a championship. In the on-air interview, head coach Aaron Glenn hugs his third-year superstar quarterback, yelling joyously to the cameras, “We’re only here because of this guy! He put us on his back and carried us to become world champions!”

The words “world champions” echo in the brain of thirty-four-year-old Miami Subs employee Zane Gonzalez as he shuts off the black-and-white television in his parents’ basement.

Zane takes in all the Miami Dolphins gear around his room – his prized foam finger from 1984, the 8-inch T.D. stuffy on his pillow – and sighs. “Where did we go wrong, T.D.?” he asks his stuffy. “How did the Jets win the Super Bowl while we’re still looking for a playoff win?”

T.D. stares at him, unblinking.

“You’re right, it was that 2027 draft. That win over the Colts knocked us out of the running for the top pick in the draft! We should have been the Super Bowl winners this year!” He looks up. “T.D., I know what I must do.”

Six months later, after convincing Dolphins owner Stephen Ross to invest $500 million in temporal engineering, Gonzalez steps into a prototype time machine and travels three years into the past.

His mission is simple: Convince the Dolphins to bring him on as placekicker. And then?

Miss.

Miss against the Patriots.

Miss against the Lions.

Most importantly: Miss against the Colts.

Make sure Miami loses enough games to stay ahead of the Colts in the draft order. Land the future franchise quarterback who would finally deliver the Dolphins’ long-awaited Super Bowl title.

Sacrifice a few meaningless wins today and the Dolphins become champions tomorrow.

After all, no one would willingly miss two field goals and an extra point in a game his team lost by two … right?

It’s January 11, 2027.

Zane Gonzalez stands at South Pointe Park Pier, staring out at the Atlantic.

The day before, the Dolphins lost to the Patriots, finishing off a 2-15 season and securing the first overall pick in the upcoming draft, one win ahead of the sad sack Colts. 

“Excuse me. Are you … Zane Gonzalez?”

He turns. A little girl, maybe six years old, stands behind him in an oversized Ricky Williams jersey. She clutches her well-loved T.D. stuffed dolphin under one arm.

“Yes,” Gonzalez says. “That’s me.”

The girl looks him up and down. Then spits at his feet.

“Nice kicking, dill weed.” Before he can respond, she pivots and marches away.

Gonzalez watches her disappear down the pier.

A smile touches the corner of his mouth.

He turns back toward the ocean.

“You’re welcome,” he whispers after her.

A single tear rolls down his cheek.

The Defense Continues To Dominate

Two weeks ago, the Dolphins held a Drake Maye-led Patriots offense to 3 points in the first half. Last week, that same defense limited Detroit’s high-powered offense to one of its lowest point totals of the season. And while the final score on Sunday will show the Colts scored 20 points, the reality is a little different. After halftime, Indianapolis managed exactly three offensive points. Daniel Jones finished with fewer than 110 passing yards. The Dolphins intercepted him twice, returned one for a touchdown, forced a fumble and repeatedly forced Indianapolis off the field with three-and-outs. By the fourth quarter, the defense was dragging the rest of the team back into the game whether it wanted to come along or not.

The usual suspects were everywhere. Chris Johnson (59-yard pick six) continues to look like one of the steals of the draft. Michael Taaffe (6 tackles, 1 pass defended) once again found ways to impact the game. Chop Robinson (1 sack, 2 QB hits) consistently disrupted the pocket. Jordyn Brooks (9 tackles, 1 pass defended) was all over the field.

The Dolphins spotted Indianapolis seven points, generated almost nothing in the kicking game, and still found themselves with a chance to win in the final minutes because the defense spent the second half strangling the Colts offense. For a unit that has carried this team for much of the season, it was another outstanding performance.

The Injury Bill Finally Came Due

Remember this scene from the greatest movie of all time?

The Dolphins’ defense is now the Bluesmobile. The Dolphins entered the game without Zach Sieler. Then Jordan Phillips got hurt, and is out for the year. Then Zeek Biggers got hurt, and he’s out for the year. By the end of the afternoon, Miami was essentially down to Kenneth Grant and Keith Cooper as healthy defensive tackles.

In-game, that degree of attrition eventually catches up with you. Without those defensive tackles, the run defense clearly felt the strain. Indianapolis finished with 172 rushing yards as Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan consistently found running lanes. The Dolphins simply didn’t have their usual flexibility up front – too many snaps played by too few healthy bodies.

Miami’s defense was good enough to win Sunday, but it wasn’t healthy enough to win Sunday.

Kyle McCord Looked Like a Rookie … and That’s OK

Let’s get the obvious part out of the way first: Kyle McCord made mistakes. The strip-sack touchdown changed the game. The late sack in the fourth quarter was costly. Neither play can simply be ignored because he’s a rookie.

But: The strip-sack wasn’t the result of panic – it was a quarterback trying to make the correct read and reacting a second too slowly. The late sack wasn’t a quarterback seeing ghosts as much as a young passer processing pressure incorrectly while trying to work deeper into the progression.

And then there’s everything else. McCord converted a third-and-13. He made several NFL-caliber throws. He stayed aggressive. And he didn’t fall apart after the strip-sack touchdown put seven points on the board for Indianapolis.

Young quarterbacks have gotten rattled by far less. Instead, McCord kept battling and gave Miami a chance to win. If you’re looking for reasons to be optimistic, Sunday’s mistakes looked fixable.

The End Is Near, and So We Face the Final Curtain

Back in August, I was so young and naïve, blinded by optimism that 2026 would lead to a glorious 6-11 season. Sure, we’re rebuilding, but at least as the youngest team in the league, we would avoid some of those devastating injuries the league’s more geriatric squads had to deal with.

Now? Now we have Kyle McCord handing the ball off to Ollie Gordon behind a leakier-than-expected offensive line. Our defensive tackles are so decimated, that we’re down to three starters – Kenneth Grant, Keith Cooper and you, dear reader. Go suit up.

The team is still in evaluation mode, and there’s still a lot of meaningful development that can and should happen for our first- and second-year starters. But the pipe dream of 6 wins feels especially unattainable now. At 38%, the Dolphins have the best odds to pick first in the 2027 draft, according to the prediction market platform Kalshi. ESPN gives the team a 41% chance, also first.

I’d like to see the Dolphins win against the Jets the Sunday after Thanksgiving. A two-win season isn’t great, but if both wins come against the Jets, that can get me through the offseason.

item.title: Interview with the Enemy: Chicago Bears
item.description: Bill Zimmerman joins us for Week 11 of IWTE.
item.content:encoded:
This week, the New Orleans Saints will head to Solider Field to face the Chicago Bears in Week 11 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Bill Zimmerman of Windy City Gridiron joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup.

NJ: How legitimate are the Bears’ Super Bowl aspirations at this point in the season? Does it feel like this could finally be the year Chicago gets it done?

BZ: The Jeffery Simmons trade changed everything as far as I’m concerned. The Bears defense was the reason they weren’t a true Super Bowl contender. Dennis Allen was largely doing it with smoke and mirrors. Yes, he had really effective blitz packages on 3rd down, but that wasn’t sustainable in the playoffs against great teams.

The offense was never a question; the defense was. With Simmons, he’s a multiplier. In just two games, we’ve seen the play improve of every defensive lineman and linebacker around him. If their front 7 can play like this, it will help a banged-up secondary that is the weakest part of the team.

No one can guarantee a Super Bowl, but I do think the Bears are on the short list of true Super Bowl contenders this year (and that’s very foreign to write).

NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Bears on Sunday against the Saints? Is there a particular area in which New Orleans could exploit?

BZ: The Bears are the healthiest they’ve been in a while heading into this game. They have RB Kyle Monangai returning, which will be a huge boost for their running game, and rookie CB Malik Muhammad may not be the biggest name, but he is a key starter in their secondary.

TE Cole Kmet is out for the year, and S Coby Bryant has been out since training camp. The only other notable starter who will be out is CB Kyler Gordon, who injured his shoulder against Tampa; he did finish the game, but he is now listed as out for this one.

The key to stopping the Bears is to attack their cornerbacks. It’s the weakest part of the roster, but you have to make sure you are getting the ball out quickly before Jeffery Simmons collapses the pocket.

NJ: How much of an impact has Dennis Allen had on turning around the Bears’ defense throughout his tenure? Have there been any decisions or coaching tendencies that have rubbed fans the wrong way?

BZ: I think Dennis Allen is very popular among Bears fans, and I think he was the perfect DC hire with Ben Johnson. I think Dennis Allen is at a point where he almost certainly isn’t going to get another head coaching job. That means he should be able to pair with Johnson and be the top coaches on this coaching staff for years to come. If things go well, they’ll have an Andy Reid/Steve Spagnuolo type partnership. 

I think, before the Simmons trade, people had been frustrated with how Dennis Allen wanted to build his defensive line, but other than that, I think Bears fans are very happy with how he calls a game, and I think most of us understand that he got a lot more success out of his defense than the level of talent that was on the field.

The best thing he’s done in Chicago is create a phenomenal third down defense. The Bears have been quite strong on third downs and it’s forcing teams to get big chunk plays on the early downs or end up punting the ball back to the Bears.

NJ: Who is one Bears player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance?

BZ: Offensively, I don’t think there are many names to give because Caleb Williams, Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, and Rome Odunze are their main weapons, and I think football fans are pretty familiar with all of them. I do think Kyle Monangai is going to be a big part of the offensive game plan and split carries with D’Andre Swift so Monangai is one returning from injury that I think can have a strong game.

Defensively, I mentioned Muhammad, but I’ll give you Austin Booker. He was a 5th-round pick in 2024 out of Missouri, and he’s been coming into his own this year as an improved run defender and a solid pass rusher. You should hear Booker’s name at least once on Sunday, either making a TFL or a sack.

NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook, the Bears (-720) are currently 11.5-point favorites over the Saints (+520) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction and how do you see the game playing out?

BZ: It’s really hard to imagine that the Bears don’t win this one. Ben Johnson is great on extra rest, and the Bears are healthy, and I don’t think it’s an insult to say the Bears are simply a better team than the Saints and are playing them at home. I think the question isn’t who will win or whether the Bears cover the big spread?

I think the offense is going to have success regardless. I think it comes down to if you think the Saints can get points on the Bears’ defense. If you do, then there’s no reason to think this one couldn’t be like 31 to 21 or so, and the Saints cover. Personally, I do think the Saints will struggle on offense against the Bears, and I think the Bears will win this one comfortably by 2 or 3 scores. I’ll call it 31 to 13.

item.title: Daiyan Henley being out with a knee injury changes nothing about the failed trade to Broncos
item.description: The failed trade of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley returned to the front burner on Friday, with the news that Henley will miss Sunday's game against the Jets due to a knee injury.
item.content:encoded:
The failed trade of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley returned to the front burner on Friday, with the news that Henley will miss Sunday's game against the Jets due to a knee injury.

It was a knee condition that prompted the Broncos to pull the plug on the deal — after trying to renegotiate the terms after the trade deadline.

From Mike Klis of 9News, who covers the Broncos: "Chargers ILB Daiyan Henley missed entire week of practices with knee injury and has been ruled out for game vs Jets. This validates concerns raised by Broncos medical team and GM George Paton. And proves Chargers were not on the up and up."

Does it really prove that the Chargers weren't "on the up and up"? The issue is that the Denver physical flagged a knee problem. In lieu of finding that the physical had been failed and that the trade won't happen, the Broncos were willing to give Henley a passing grade, if the compensation was changed.

Henley has played every game this season. He played on Monday night against the Ravens. As far as anyone knows, he injured the knee during that game.

As far as anyone knows, the currently injured knee isn't the same knee that created the concern during the Denver physical.

It's all just noise at this point. The core problem is the ability of a team — after the trade deadline has passed — to renegotiate the terms of a trade. And the related issue is the ability of a team to give a conditional grade on the pass-fail question of a physical that is tied to the specific compensation.

A player either passes the physical, or he fails it. The process shouldn't include an epilogue premised on the outcome of the physical being "maybe." Especially after the time for negotiating trades has ended.

item.title: 3 Keys to Victory for Ravens-Panthers in Week 11
item.description: The Ravens have dropped five in a row. Can they avoid six in a row and keep their slim playoff hopes alive?
item.content:encoded:
This is it. You can’t finish with a record of 11-6 until you first reach 5-6. Technically, the Ravens could make the playoffs with seven or eight losses — but this feels like a defining moment. With the Houston Texans on the rise, Tampa Bay’s roster built perfectly to beat the Ravens, and then four division games in a row, this game against Carolina feels like the easiest one remaining on the schedule. If the Ravens lose, any little fleeting hope for a run will fizzle. It’s been a drama-filled week for the Ravens, and they’ll be missing Nnamdi Madubuike, so they need to figure out how to put their heads down and grind out this win to avoid dropping six in a row.

Find the formation that works

The Ravens have run multiple tight end sets at the seventh-highest rate this year, 43.6% of the time, according to Next Gen Stats. They are largely successful throwing out of these sets as well, averaging 8.1 yards per pass attempt, which is 12th-most in the league. The issue is they pass out of 12 and 13 personnel less than 40% of the time, according to SumerSports. This both inflates their pass success rate and shows they are running more than 60% of the time out of these formations, allowing defenses to key in on the run. Recently, Declan Doyle has had an issue with running out of heavy on first down too frequently, making it very obvious and setting the Ravens behind the chains.

The Ravens need to start mixing it up more. That could mean throwing out of heavy on early downs more often to catch the Panthers by surprise. The biggest issue there is that the Panthers have allowed the third-fewest yards per attempt against multi-tight end sets (5.8). The real solution might just be to lean on Jacoby Brissetts arm, play more 11 personnel, and sling the ball around the field to Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman and Ja’Kobi Lane. The Panthers have been down their top three cornerbacks for a while. Rookie Will Lee is expected to return in this one, but Jaycee Horn remains on IR and Mike Jackson, while practicing this week, hasn’t been activated yet. The Ravens might want to test whoever is covering their wide receivers. Spreading the offense out in 11 might help the run game as well if the Ravens can find success early through the air and back the Panthers off the line of scrimmage and out of the box.

Finishes from Mike Green and Trey Hendrickson

Hendrickson leads the Ravens in pressures despite missing two games and dealing with a figure injury since Week 1. He’s also getting double-teamed 42% of his pass rush snaps, according to ESPN. He also only has two sacks through his first eight games as a Raven, and that simply isn’t good enough or what the Ravens paid for. Conversely, the Ravens have seen Green get better throughout this season while going through some ups and downs, switching from one side of the defensive front to the other. He leads the Ravens in sacks with 5.5. The Panthers’ biggest overall weakness is their offensive line.

Both of Carolina’s offensive tackles have been question marks this season. Their rookie right tackle, Monroe Freeling, has a 6-foot-7 frame with speed and athleticism, but the transition from left tackle in college to right in the NFL hasn’t been without questions. Rasheed Walker on the left side has struggled this season and given up a chunk of sacks as well. Without Madubuike, the Ravens need their two top edge rushers to get pressures and, more importantly, finish.

Middle of the field defense

It’s no surprise to anyone who watches Ravens games that their defense has given up a lot over the middle of the field. They’ve also been the worst defense on intermediate passes, giving up a league-worst 0.77 EPA per play on passes between 10 and 19 yards. Furthermore, the Ravens have been targeted on in-breaking routes on 36.7% of opponents’ passes, giving up seven touchdowns on them, 10th most in the league according to Next-Gen Stats. Meanwhile, the Panthers have four different 6-foot-4 wide receivers, and Bryce Young has thrown in-breakers on 38.8% of his routes, averaging 9.0 yards per attempt on these routes. That’s a lot of size and a lot of attempts for Roquan Smith to cover over the middle.

Jesse Minter’s defense is designed to leave the middle of the field open; it’s the hardest area of the field to consistently throw in, with the most bodies, hands, arms, and heads to navigate. The idea is to funnel passes there, force as many tough throws as possible, and then have 11 hats on the ball to tackle quickly when passes do get caught there. It hasn’t worked so far. The Ravens players haven’t executed it consistently all season, and Minter has yet to deviate from it. Something has to change, and this would be a great game to make changes for it.

item.title: Can the Rams add anyone to replace Puka Nacua?
item.description: No one will replace Puka Nacua and other NFL news
item.content:encoded:
Should the Los Angeles Rams have a traded for a wide receiver at the trade deadline with Puka Nacua expected to be out? Was anyone available going to replace Nacua? Likely not. Nacua’s injury is a loss to the Rams no matter who they could’ve added via trade.

Will the Rams be able to overcome the loss of Nacua? Anything can happen, but likely not exactly. Nacua offered an incredible offensive presence and he’s out now. There is no easy answer. The Rams will just have to put in the work and play their best.

Will it be enough? They’ll find out.

Rams WR Puka Nacua had MCL surgery, likely to miss rest of season (ramswire)

“McVay says he will miss a couple of months, which means he probably won’t play again this season.

Initially, Nacua was placed on IR but was expected to return in mid-December after missing the minimum of four games. But that was before the Rams realized he needed surgery, which will prolong his rehab. Nacua is scheduled to be a free agent in March.

“Puka Nacua decided to get surgery on his MCL on Tuesday, so that’ll be a couple of months for him,” McVay said.“

Injury Updates: Puka Nacua out for ‘couple months’ as he will undergo MCL surgery; Kobie Turner expected to return to practice; latest on Terrance Ferguson, Davante Adams and Justin Dedich (therams.com)

‘Additionally, defensive end Kobie Turner is expected to return to practice and the Rams will open his 21-day practice window this week after sustaining a Week 6 groin injury that landed him on Injured Reserve. McVay added, “hopefully he’ll be ready to go this week.”

With regard to tight end Terrance Ferguson (ankle/hamstring) and wide receiver Davante Adams (hamstring)’s potential returns in Week 12, McVay said “we’re not quite there yet.”

After an ankle injury in Week 4 led to the Rams placing Ferguson on IR, he started his 21-day practice window in the week leading up to Week 9, but picked up a hamstring injury during the Friday practice before the Commanders game. Ferguson missed Week 9 and Week 10 before the bye week. McVay said the plan is to still bring Ferguson onto the active roster before that 21-day window closes so he doesn’t have to be shut down for the season.“

Rams WR Puka Nacua has knee surgery, likely out for season, McVay says (spectrumnews1)

“McVay had expressed optimism last week that Nacua could return to the field this season, but he said the star wideout decided this week to have surgery, which was performed Tuesday. Nacua is in the final year of his rookie contract and is eligible to sign a large extension.

“I kind of thought when the initial injury occurred that this was more likely the direction that this would go, so this isn’t anything necessarily new on our end,” McVay said. “He had to get some different information, talk to people, and there’s a lot of conversations that go into whether you’re going to do that or not, and what’s the best plan of action for return to performance for him — not exclusive to this year, but for his career moving forward.”

Nacua received a three-game suspension from the NFL on Thursday for violating its personal conduct policies. His suspension will expire during his mandated four-game stint on injured reserve, but the knee surgery will keep him out much longer.“

Packers Catch Huge Break Ahead of Must-Win Rams Showdown (sports.yahoo)

“The Packers’ loss to the Vikings dropped their playoff odds to just 35 percent, and Green Bay’s next game, which comes against the Los Angeles Rams on November 25, will determine whether the Packers’ chances at a fourth consecutive trip to the postseason spike to 58 percent or plummet to 23 percent.

That doesn’t necessarily render Green Bay’s return to the gridiron five days from now a must-win, but the path to the playoffs gets murky with a loss to the Rams on Thanksgiving Eve — not only because it will drop the Packers to 6-5 and take the division almost entirely out of play, but because the Rams are likely to prove prime competition for one of the last wildcard spots in the NFC and will hold the head-to-head tiebreaker with a victory.“

Rams WR Puka Nacua has surgery on MCL and is likely OUT for the 2026 season | ‘The NFL Report’ (nfl.com)

“Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua had surgery to repair an MCL and will likely miss the remainder of the 2026 NFL season.”

Rams should have all the convincing they need to commit to CJ Daniels (ramblinfan)

“Even with Adams back, the Rams can no longer treat Daniels as a placeholder to be discarded upon Nacua’s return. Instead, they have every reason to continue his development in earnest for the remainder of the season.

Rams have little to lose by doubling down on CJ Daniels

Despite flashes from veteran Tutu Atwell and a team-leading Week 10 performance from Konata Mumpfield,
the Rams have not gotten consistent contributions beneath Adams and Nacua on the receiver depth chart. Disappointingly, Atwell has been plagued by a bout of drops.“

One questionable play call may have crushed Rams’ Super Bowl chances (ramswire)

“McVay even admitted a day after the game that he was “kicking” himself for that play call and has questioned the decision “over and over,” knowing the consequences of losing Nacua. That was almost two weeks ago, before the Rams knew Nacua needed surgery.

“I’m kicking myself about those things,” he said. “… I’d be lying to you if I said I haven’t questioned the decision making on that last play over and over in my head of what could have been another option that you felt like could have gotten a conversion and maybe end of the game that would have led to him not taking a violent hit to his right knee. It’s stuff that I feel tremendous responsibility for, and we have to be able to figure out how to protect these guys while also putting them in positions that help our team and allow them to be able to shine.”

Sean McVay discusses injury updates, evolving the Rams’ offense, preparing for Week 12 & more (therams.com)

“Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay discusses injury updates, continuing to evolve the Rams’ offense, preparing for Week 12 against the Green Bay Packers, and more.”

Puka Nacua Injury Exposes Rams’ Biggest Roster Management Failure (si.com)

“Ferguson couldn’t make it through one full practice after the Rams opened his practice window before injuring his hamstring. Adams underwent surgery on his hamstring, but it’s the same one that has bothered him for the last two years 

It’s always easy to look at roster decisions with the benefit of hindsight. With that said, depth at the wide receiver position is something that the Rams have needed since the early spring. 

Rams’ Failure to Address Wide Receiver Depth Was Always a Risk

Ignoring the position and banking on injury-prone players to stay healthy always felt like roster mismanagement. Now, the Rams are set to enter the hardest part of their schedule and will be relying on players like Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, Xavier Smith, and CJ Daniels.“ 

Seahawks Dealt Favorable Rams Twist in NFC West Race: Insider (nfl.com)

“Asked whether the receiver’s regular season was over, McVay said, “You can pretty much say yes.”

Jeremiah looked at the schedule during an appearance on “The Rich Eisen Show”. Seattle still has both games against Los Angeles ahead of it.

“They’re not gonna have to deal with Puka twice,” Jeremiah said. “They’re the biggest winners in this whole thing.”

item.title: Future Broncos: 3 Prospects to Watch in Week 12 of NCAA Football Season
item.description: Here are three collegiate players Broncos Country should watch today in Week 12 of the NCAA Football Season.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to another installment of Future Broncos. We are getting down to the final weeks of the collegiate football season before the playoffs and bowl games begin. Another Saturday, another big slate of games for fans to enjoy. Here are three prospects of interest Broncos Country should keep their eye on today.

Sammy Omosigho — Linebacker — UCLA

The Broncos tried to make a splash prior to the NFL trade deadline making a deal for Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley. Unfortunately, the medical review of Henley’s knee wasn’t favorable and the trade wound up being nixed. That saved the Broncos a fourth and fifth round selection in the 2027 NFL Draft. However, it’s clear they are hoping to upgrade the position long-term given their interest in Henley.

I haven’t covered too many inside linebackers in this year’s class. However, UCLA prospect Sammy Omosigho is one that is skyrocketing up draft boards. Omosigho started his collegiate career at Oklahoma back in 2023 and spent his first three seasons there.

He never earned a full-time starting role in their defense but was a quality contributor in the snaps he played. In 36 games with the Sooners, he amassed 96 tackles, 10 tackles for loss, 2 sacks, 1 forced fumble, and one fumble recovery. For his final season, he transferred to UCLA and has become one of the best playmakers in their defense.

A ten-game starter for the Bruins, Omosigho (6’2”, 239 pounds) has been on an absolute tear as a senior. He already has 72 tackles, 10.5 tackles for loss, 5.5 sacks, and a whopping five forced fumbles. Whether it’s stuffing the run, getting after the passer, or doing well in coverage—he touts some of the best numbers of any draft eligible prospect.

Given his versatility, I think he is a player Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph and the Broncos’ scouts are going to be keeping a close eye on throughout the draft evaluation process. You can catch Omosigho in action today when the undefeated and fourth ranked Bruins take on the Michigan Wolverines on CBS. If he keeps playing at a high level, he should easily be a Day 2 selection next April.

Ty Benefield — Safety — LSU

This past week, the Broncos opted to extend boundary cornerback Riley Moss. The $67 million deal will keep him in orange and blue for the next for seasons. While Denver’s boundary duo is set for the foreseeable future, the long-term outlook at safety is far less certain.

The reason is simple; Brandon Jones is a free agent and has regressed this season. Moreover, Talanoa Hufanga’s contract is up after the 2027 season. Keep in mind most all of their depth players are on one-year contracts as well. There is no doubt in my mind Denver will be addressing the long-term need there in the 2027 NFL Draft.

One player that is having a tremendous senior season is LSU safety Ty Benefield. Benefield is the son of Daved Benefield, who was a thirteen-year linebacker and All-Star player in the Canadian Football League. Ty was a backup player and pinch starter as a freshman for the Broncos in 2023 but earned a full-time role as a starter for his sophomore and junior campaigns.

In three seasons at Boise State, he played in 41 games with 33 starts and put up some eye-popping numbers: 235 tackles, 18 tackles for loss, 3 sacks, 5 interceptions, 4 fumble recoveries, and 2 forced fumbles. This year, he transferred to LSU to see if he could improve his draft stock and battle much tougher competition in the SEC.

So far, so good for Benefield (6’3”, 216 pounds). In my opinion, has been one of the best defensive backs in the nation. In ten games, he has 49 tackles, 4.5 sacks and 3 interceptions. With some injuries in their secondary, he has seen time at both safety and nickelback. That positional versatility will be valued by NFL scouts and general managers and should be of interest to Denver giving the ambiguity at both positions moving forward.

His physical profile is off the charts, and he has consistently produced at a high level. I think he is one of the most well-rounded defensive backs in this class and a great fit for Joseph’s aggressive defense. If he keeps dominating, I don’t think being picked in the Top 50 is out of the question for him come spring. You can catch Benefield in action this afternoon when the Tigers take on the ninth-ranked Tennessee Volunteers on ABC.

Wayshawn Parker — Running Back — Utah

I haven’t covered too many running backs in Future Broncos. I remain quite bullish on the potential of Jonah Coleman and RJ Harvey as the future thunder and lightning duo for the offense. However, both have had some injuries this season and J.K. Dobbins has not looked as good as he did in the first half of 2025 prior to injury.

I kind of treat running back in drafts like MLB teams approach pitching. It’s always worth pursuing and better to have and need than need and not have. Strong rushing attacks are what get you through the late half of the season and are extremely important come the playoffs.

A particular underclassman that has caught my eyes in a few games this season is Utah Utes junior Wayshawn Parker. Parker started his career out at Washington State. In twelve contests as a freshman, he had 137 carries for 735 yards and 4 touchdowns. He added 11 receptions for 108 yards and a touchdown as a receiver.

For his sophomore season, he transferred to Utah and saw an uptick in playing production. Parker had 981 yards and 6 touchdowns on 149 carries. His 6.6 yard per carry average was the best in the Big 12. He caught 13 passes for 185 yards and 3 touchdowns and had 1,166 all-purpose yards.

In 10 games this season, Parker (6’0″, 199 pounds) has 764 rushing yards and 9 rushing touchdowns. He also has been more involved in their passing attack under the new coaching regime and sports 29 catches for 269 yards and 4 touchdowns.

Based on what I’ve seen, he is one of the best draft-eligible backs when it comes to forcing missed tackles (49 last season) and getting yards after contact. He is a dual threat player that offers a lot of value as a runner and receiver out of the backfield. For those of you who are wondering about his pass protection? It’s quite good for just a junior player.

I’m not sure Parker ends up declaring, but he is definitely on my radar. I think he would add a lot of juice and playmaking ability for the Broncos. He has been a big reason for Utah’s success on offense this season. You can catch Parker and the second-ranked Utes in action when they take on TCU tomorrow evening.
