item.content:encoded:
Ben Fitzsimmons asks: I know Matt Nagy is the OC and is the one calling plays. I don’t fully understand how Greg Roman fits into it. We’ve seen the Giants run it between the tackles at least 400 million times on first down this year. We’ve seen that terrible play from the infamous JJ Package show up a few times (still hasn’t worked once btw). We’ve seen the Giants attempt and fail miserably to run the clock out at the end of games multiple times this year. We’ve seen a lack of creativity in the run game as they mostly just run behind Ricard and hope it works (it usually doesn’t).

What I’m curious about is how much of that is Greg Roman and how much is Matt Nagy. Is Roman designing the run plays and Matt Nagy is just calling them? Is Roman just providing advice and vibes while Nagy draws up the plays? Does Roman have any impact on how run plays are called each game (I would assume not, but I’ve been wrong many times before)?

Ed says: Ben, Greg Roman’s title is ‘Senior Offensive Assistant’. Nagy runs the offense and makes all play-calling decisions. He makes final determination, with John Harbaugh’s input, on the game plan. Roman is acknowledged as one of the best run-game designers in the game today. To my knowledge, Roman is responsible for designing much of the Giants’ run game.

Harbaugh has explained that much of the vertical passing game comes from Nagy’s background. As I’ve said, Roman’s specialty is the run game.

Nagy’s job, as he has explained it, is to take the menu of options he has in front of him and decide what to use and when to use it. Roman, who has been an offensive coordinator multiple times, sits in the booth with Nagy on game days. Of course there will be some sharing of information and ideas. The decisions, though, are Nagy’s to make.

We see the warts. Sometimes, you make the wrong call. Sometimes, you make the right one and players don’t execute it. The Giants are 14th in the league in score at 22.6 points per game. That’s pretty good, considering that they are on their third quarterback and have struggled mightily to block in the run game.

Bob Donnelly asks: Following the Commanders’ game you have questioned some of the offensive play calls, especially not running the ball in a few key situations.  The OC makes the play call yet much of the blame/criticism seems to be directed towards the HC and his lack of confidence in his team’s ability to run the ball in those situations.

In your view how much play calling influence does our head coach exert in critical situations?

Ed says: Bob, the reality is that the head coach gets credit when things go right, and everything that goes wrong also lands at his feet.

Harbaugh does not call the plays. He can set the direction, though. Does he want the ball run? Thrown? What personnel does he want in the game.

Tom Donlan asks: Malik Nabers can make spectacular catches and carry the passing game with a high volume of targets and catches. We’ve also seen drops and a costly fumble against Washington, as well as what some view as immature or disruptive behavior with poor body language on the field. What do you think he needs to do to become a more consistent No. 1 receiver, and do you know how the Giants view the way he voices his frustrations publicly?

Ed says: Tom, Malik Nabers has a drop rate this season of 3.5%, per Pro Football Reference. That isn’t exactly terrible. He has fumbled three times in 185 career touches, one basically every 62 touches. Again, that isn’t awful. Drops happen occasionally. No one who has the ball a lot goes through a career without fumbling at times.

I’m not getting into the body language debate. As far as becoming a more consistent No. 1 receiver, how about getting some consistent reps with the quarterback. Nabers barely had any time with Jaxson Dart last year. Nabers’ reps were limited all summer as he came back from his knee injury, then Dart went down for the season in Week 2. Now, Nabers and J.J. McCarthy have worked together for a month.

My educated guess is the Giants would like him to choose his words more carefully. But, he was encouraged to speak his mind freely as a rookie, and he is still a 23-year-old kid learning to grow up with a much different coach than the one who drafted him.

One other thing I will say is that I still believe Nabers has to learn to do a better job fighting to protect his quarteerback. I’m thinking about that interception at the end of the Washington game. The receiver simply has to put up a fight there to make sure the ball gets knocked down and not intercepted.

Joel Story asks: I read an article saying that after the Giants/Eagles game on Nov. 8th, Kayvon Thibodeaux was fined $11,941 for taunting, Jeremiah Trotter was fined $6,428 for tripping, Zack Baun was fined $6,750 for illegal use of the helmet, and Andrew Mukuba was fined $9,041 for a hit on a defenseless player. Are these amounts correct? If so, do you know why the NFL/NFLPA have chosen to fine players more for taunting than for the other three actions which could potentially end other players’ seasons or even their careers?

Ed says: Joel, yes those amounts are correct. The fine schedule, which you can see it for yourself, is collectively bargained.

Taj Siddiqi asks: JH is being criticized for keeping Dominic Zvada and let Jason Sanders walk. Sanders is performing like a pro while Zvada is struggling. Some people think one of the causes for his firing at Baltimore was his decision to stay with the kicker, whose name I can’t recall. Is JH over confident regarding his ability to evaluate kickers? Is the guy at the Baltimore still there or is he even in the league?

Ed says: Taj, John Harbaugh has been around long enough to fully understand the ups and downs, and the risks, of choosing to ride with a rookie placekicker.

Harbaugh had a rookie placekicker in Baltimore last season. Tyler Loop was very good for the Ravens in 2025. He made 30 of 34 field goals (88.2%). Harbaugh got fired because the Ravens missed the playoffs and the organization felt like his tenure had run its course after 18 years. It just so happens that Loop missed a 44-yard field goal on the final play of that game that would have gotten Baltimore into the playoffs. It was his only miss of the year between 40 and 49 yards.

How does anyone criticize a coach for riding with a kicker who went 30 of 34? Loop is still with the Ravens, but he is injured and on IR.

Overconfident in his ability to evaluate kickers? Well, he and the Ravens drafted Jordan Stout in the fourth round in 2022. Stout is probably the best punter in the league. Sam Koch punted in Baltimore for 16 years, 14 of those for Harbaugh.

Justin Tucker was the best field goal kicker in the NFL for more than a decade, and was bombing 60+ yard kicks long before there were a bunch of other kickers in the league capable of doing it. I would say Harbaugh knows good kickers when he sees them. If Harbaugh ends up being wrong about Zvada, that will be the first kicker or punter he has been wrong about in his time as a head coach.

As for Jason Sanders, I saw a number of those practices in the spring. A day or two before he got cut I watched him try to kick a 50-ish yard field goal on a windy day, and I watched the ball basically die and go straight down a couple yards short. I didn’t think he could handle the MetLife Stadium conditions, either.

Francis Castros asks: Can you provide the rehabilitation status of the following players and are they required to rehab at the Quest Diagnostics Training Center?

  – Tyrone Tracy Jr. — RB (Hamstring)
  – Tremaine Edmunds — LB / MLB (Chest / Shoulder)
  – Braxton Berrios — WR (Foot – surgery)
  – Chauncey Golston — DE / Edge (Neck)
  – Jaxson Dart — QB (Knee – Meniscus)
  – Brian Burns — LB (Knee – ACL)
  – Roy Robertson-Harris — DE (Achilles)
  – Calvin Austin III — WR (Knee)
  – Rico Payton — CB (Undisclosed)
  – Jarrick Bernard-Converse — CB (Knee)
  – Gunner Olszewski — WR (Achilles)
  – Thaddeus Dixon — CB (Achilles)

Ed says: Francis, I really don’t have much. The team is not required to, and does not, share information about players on IR.

I can tell you Tyrone Tracy should be back at some point in the next few weeks. I saw Brian Burns in the locker room after the Washington game. He is still on crutches. Jaxson Dart has been seen at the facility a couple of times by media, though I have not seen him myself. I have seen Roy Robertson-Harris around a couple of times.

Players are not required to rehab at the team facility. Many do, though, spend at least some of their time doing that.

Wesley Protheroe asks: I have a question regarding the utilization of the Giants’ tight ends:

While Isaiah Likely has been outstanding, the Giants’ “conventional” tight ends have been largely ineffective.  Johnson is an unreliable pass catcher and only a fair blocker. Manhertz is a better blocker but has only one target all season and defenses don’t have to account for him. Fidone has been mostly a healthy scratch but has shown good hands in the pre-season and caught his one target for 29 yards. Shouldn’t the Giants consider replacing Manhertz with an interior lineman or at least throw to him periodically to keep defenses honest?  Additionally, why not give Fidone a chance to play over Johnson. He is definitely the more natural receiver.  Your thoughts?

Ed says: Wesley, the Giants are not going to intentionally throw to Chris Manhertz when they can throw to Malik Nabers, Isaiah Likely, Malachi Fields, or Darnell Mooney instead. Still, if he runs out in a pass pattern he does have to be covered.

I’m not replacing Manhertz with an offensive lineman who isn’t used to being out on the end of the line of scrimmage. Honestly, though, while I can’t point to specific plays it does feel to me like neither Manhertz nor Patrick Ricard are having the impact on the run game the Giants were hoping for.

In reference to Johnson vs. Fidone, I am curious if Fidone could play a bigger role. It is pretty clear, though, that the coaching staff prefers Johnson. Maybe part of the reason is that Johnson has also become a fairly significant part of the special teams.

David Silver asks: A lot of articles this week were taking a look at Abdul Carter, trying to make sense of his game. By any measure but sacks, he has been a destructive, disruptive force who makes quarterbacks uncomfortable, including a third-best speed to the QB of 2.97 seconds. It seems when he’s not getting us a holding call, the QB is unloading the ball when they see him destroying another lineman. My question is, how often do the rush Carter from the blindside? I mean, if he is one of the fastest rushers to the QB in the league, what happens when you can’t see him coming? More sacks, right?

Ed says: David, I don’t have access to data on exactly where each of Carter’s pass rushes come from. I’m sure it exists somewhere, but not in anything I have available.

What I can tell you is that Carter has played 503 defensive snaps, and has been used in a multitude of positions. He has been used 167 times at right outside linebacker, and 157 at left outside linebacker. That leaves 179 snaps where he has been aligned in a variety of other places, from nose tackle to middle linebacker.

From that, you have to extrapolate that defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson is already doing a good job moving Carter around.

Bruce Frazer asks: Donte Whitner on ESPN described JJ McCarthy as a one read quarterback, not ready to elevate the giants to a higher level. He showed a number of plays highlighting the problem showing JJ constantly keying on his first read and throwing to that receiver. Do you feel this is an issue that the coaches are aware of this.

Ed says: Bruce, c’mon now! This has been McCarthy’s reputation since his Michigan days. It’s hardly a revelation. He threw far less in college than the other quarterbacks in that draft class. He’s played in 15 NFL games — less than a full season. This is a common issue with young, inexperienced quarterbacks. Of course the coaching staff is aware of it.

Submit a question

Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

item.title: Bears Week 11 Flashbacks: Ditka’s Revenge, Butler’s Boot, Jets Shutout
item.description: Hop aboard the Gridiron Time Machine with @iamcogs and take a trip down Week 11 Bears memory lane!
item.content:encoded:
Climb aboard the Gridiron Time Machine as we revisit three memorable Week 11 performances from Chicago Bears history!

1.) 1985, Bears @ Cowboys: Ditka gets the last laugh

November 17, 1985 | Bears win 44-0

The 1985 Chicago Bears entered Week 11 undefeated at 10-0, but their trip to Dallas carried a little extra significance for head coach Mike Ditka.

Waiting on the opposite sideline was Tom Landry, the legendary Cowboys coach who had brought Ditka onto his coaching staff after his playing career ended.

By the time the afternoon was over, Landry probably wished his former assistant had stayed home.

The Bears wasted little time making their presence felt. Richard Dent intercepted a deflected Danny White pass and returned it one yard for a touchdown to open the scoring. Mike Richardson joined the fun in the second quarter, returning another interception 36 yards for a score.

Chicago led 24-0 at halftime, and things weren’t about to get any better for Dallas.

The Bears’ defense intercepted four passes, recovered a fumble and sacked Cowboys quarterbacks six times. Dallas managed just 171 total yards, including a miserable 52 on the ground, while converting only three of its 13 third-down opportunities.

Walter Payton handled business on the offensive side, rushing for 132 yards on 22 carries. Chicago finished with 216 rushing yards and 378 total yards of offense, while Kevin Butler connected on all three of his field goal attempts.

The Bears scored another 20 points in the second half, including fourth-quarter touchdown runs from Calvin Thomas and Dennis Gentry, turning an already embarrassing afternoon into a historic beatdown.

Chicago walked out of Texas Stadium with a 44-0 victory, improving to 11-0 and clinching the NFC Central championship.

Four interceptions, two defensive touchdowns and a 44-point shutout against America’s Team.

Not a bad way to remind your former boss how far you’ve come.

2.) 1990, Bears @ Broncos: Butler gets a second chance

November 18, 1990 | Bears win 16-13 (OT)

The Bears entered Week 11 of the 1990 season at 8-1, riding a five-game winning streak and looking like one of the best teams in the NFC.

A trip to Mile High Stadium against John Elway and the Denver Broncos would prove to be anything but easy.

Chicago’s offense struggled to find the end zone for much of the afternoon, settling for a pair of Kevin Butler field goals before Brad Muster finally broke through with a 10-yard touchdown run late in the third quarter.

The score gave Chicago a 13-6 advantage heading into the final period.

Unfortunately, Elway wasn’t finished.

The Broncos quarterback scrambled nine yards for a touchdown early in the fourth quarter, tying the game at 13 and setting up a tense finish.

Chicago had an opportunity to win in regulation, but Butler’s 41-yard field goal attempt struck the left upright.

Not exactly the ending the Bears had in mind.

Fortunately, overtime gave Butler an opportunity to make up for the miss.

After the Bears got the ball back with favorable field position, Butler stepped onto the field and drilled a 44-yard field goal to secure a 16-13 victory.

While Butler supplied the game-winning points, Chicago’s ground game did much of the heavy lifting. Neal Anderson rushed for 110 yards on 28 carries, helping the Bears pile up 202 rushing yards and control the football for more than 40 minutes.

The defense also made life difficult for Elway, recording six sacks and forcing two turnovers while holding Denver to just 108 rushing yards.

Chicago escaped Mile High Stadium with its sixth consecutive victory, improving to 9-1 on the season.

A missed game-winner, an overtime opportunity and a kicker who made sure he didn’t miss twice.

Sometimes all you need is a second chance.

3.) 2006, Bears @ Jets: The defense does it again

November 19, 2006 | Bears win 10-0

The 2006 Chicago Bears were already 8-1 when they traveled to the Meadowlands for a Week 11 matchup with the New York Jets.

They were also beginning to establish a familiar formula for winning football games.

Play outstanding defense, run the football and hope Rex Grossman doesn’t make things too interesting.

Against the Jets, that formula worked just fine.

Neither offense managed to score in the first half, with Chicago struggling to move the football through the air and New York finding little success against Lovie Smith’s defense.

Grossman completed just 11-of-22 passes for 119 yards on the afternoon, while the Bears converted only four of their 14 third-down opportunities.

Fortunately, Thomas Jones was there to keep the offense moving.

Jones rushed for 121 yards on 23 carries, helping Chicago accumulate 173 yards on the ground. The Bears finished with 284 total yards of offense, but points remained difficult to come by.

Robbie Gould finally broke the scoreless tie with a 20-yard field goal in the third quarter, giving Chicago a 3-0 lead.

Then, early in the fourth quarter, Grossman connected with Mark Bradley for a 57-yard touchdown that provided some much-needed breathing room.

That was more than enough for the Bears’ defense.

Chicago intercepted Jets quarterback Chad Pennington twice, with Brian Urlacher and Nathan Vasher each recording a takeaway. Pennington finished with just 162 passing yards, and New York managed only 264 total yards despite running nine more offensive plays than Chicago.

The Jets also converted just six of their 17 third-down attempts as the Bears secured their second shutout of the season.

Chicago walked away with a 10-0 victory, improving to 9-1 and continuing its march toward Super Bowl XLI.

Ten points, 119 passing yards and another victory.

Who needs an explosive offense when the other team can’t score?

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Why this year is different for 49ers superstar Christian McCaffrey
item.description: No wonder Christian McCaffrey looks fresh. The responsibility to carry the ball no longer exclusively falls on his shoulders.
item.content:encoded:
Christian McCaffrey has made it clear: If it were up to him, he’d take all the handoffs.

At 30 years old, in his 10th season, he has also been around the block enough to know that his personal desires aren’t necessarily what’s best for the team’s ultimate goal.

And that is something that all 53 players in the 49ers’ locker room agree on:

What happens in Weeks 1 through 18 isn’t how they’ll judge this season. What’s going to make or break a successful season is what happens from then on.

It’s the same goal that this veteran-laden team has had basically going back to Kyle Shanahan’s hiring 10 seasons ago.

And, like every other year, the 49ers will lean heavily on McCaffrey to get there.

What’s different this time? McCaffrey may just be hitting his stride at just the right time.

The 49ers earned a lot of attention for their total offensive output in Sunday’s shootout win over the Cowboys — 584 yards — as well as the portion for which McCaffrey was responsible.

The game was the Niners’ most productive under Shanahan, arguably the NFL’s best offensive coach, and their do-it-all running back accounted for almost 40% of it.

McCaffrey went off for 223 yards — 62 on the ground, 161 through the air — an impressive showing if there ever was one. It was McCaffrey’s third-highest total of his career and the most yards from scrimmage a 49ers player has accumulated since Frank Gore’s 244-yard game in 2009. Nobody had racked up 200-plus yards and three touchdowns besides Jerry Rice.

But here’s the number that the 49ers Faithful should really care about:

Seventeen.

That’s the number of touches McCaffrey required to eclipse 200 yards. Catch-and-runs of 74 and 66 yards for scores, as well as another 16-yard touchdown scamper, will help with that.

Here’s another: 

Sixty-eight.

That’s the percentage of the 49ers’ offensive snaps this season that McCaffrey has been on the field. In other words, almost one-third of the plays Shanahan has drawn up haven’t involved McCaffrey at all. That’s 31% of plays that McCaffrey isn’t taking bruising hits, exerting himself or putting further strain on the ligaments and muscles that will carry the 49ers’ load come January.

That’s a far cry from McCaffrey’s NFL-high 413 touches last season. He was on the field for 83% of the 49ers’ snaps last year, or 932 total plays. 

This season, he’s on pace to log more than 200 fewer plays by the end of the regular season.

No wonder he looks fresh.

The responsibility to carry the ball no longer exclusively falls on his shoulders.

“As talents and as people,” Shanahan said, “I think they pair together very well.”

That’s not something that would have come out of the coach’s mouth last season, when McCaffrey was their only trusted ball carrier (and still struggled, averaging fewer than 4 yards per carry for his first time with the 49ers). This year, he’s averaging 4.5 yards per carry, his most efficient running since he was Offensive Player of the Year in 2023.

As soon as McCaffrey met the running back they drafted 90th overall out of Indiana, he knew this season had a chance to be different.

McCaffrey saw a kindred spirit in Kaelon Black. He’s lived up to the billing.

“I think Christian really respects Kaelon,” Shanahan said. “I remember Christian telling me right when he got here how much of a pro that guy seemed like and seemed like he was made of the right stuff. It’s because K.B., similar to Christian, he works at everything. He’s very hard on himself. He’s very tough and approaches each day to get better.”

Shanahan called McCaffrey the “perfect mentor.” In Black, he found a subject worthy of his wisdom. At 25 years old, he has a maturity not typically found in first-year players.

And as a bruising back who does his best work outside the tackles, he’s the perfect backfield partner for McCaffrey. He’s racked up 186 yards on 34 rushing attempts the past three weeks.

McCaffrey, meanwhile, has taken 38 handoffs for 169 yards over that same span. Shanahan’s trust in Black has freed up McCaffrey to contribute more in the passing game, hauling in 12 passes for 241 yards to help offset Mike Evans’ absence.

McCaffrey is still the 49ers’ most important weapon in an offense full of them.

It’s in everyone’s best interests that his fuel tank is as full as possible come the playoffs.

Then again, the way Black is running, the 49ers seem dangerous no matter who’s taking the handoffs.

“We love our room,” McCaffrey said last week. “I think with KB, when he comes in it’s such a spark. When I can come in and come out and get my wind, he goes in, balls out, comes out, gets his wind. If we can just continue to do that, man, I think we can be really special.”

item.title: The Day After the Day After: Houston Texans stomp the Indianapolis Colts on Thursday Night
item.description: Too little, too late? Regardless, a satisfying 26-3 beatin’ of the Ponies is always good for the Texans’ fan soul.
item.content:encoded:
The Textbook Texans’ Sequence: If the Texans could script their ideal game sequence, look no further than what happened between the 11:55 and 4:19 marks of the 3rd Quarter. It started with Kai Kroeger, whose punting has been sporadic at best, uncorking a 56-yard punt that landed out of bounds at the IND 5. This put the Colts in bad field position, allowing the Texans’ defense to go on the attack. Two plays yielded only 2 yards for the Colts. On 3rd and long, the Colts wisely thought to double Will Anderson Jr. However, Anderson soundly beat that double team, all but driving the tackle right into Jones, as Anderson turned that sack into a safety. On the subsequent possession, Houston used a Smith 32-yard kick return to start at their 43. From there, Houston used a 10-play (6 run/4 pass), 57-yard drive that took over 6 minutes off the clock and ended in a TD that put the Texans up 23. Strong special teams, dominant defense and a steady, scoring offense. When a team is 4-6, that usually means the ideal hasn’t happened a lot.

The End of the Jones Era: The Texans’ defense beating of the Colts was so severe, it reverberated beyond the gridiron. As the second half wore on, sideline cameras showed visible frustration between QB Daniel Jones and HC Shane Steichen, as the Colts proved unable to move the ball. After an 87-yard, 3-point 1st quarter, the Colts only managed 80 yards and no points over the next 3. On the Colts’ final offensive possession, Jones gave way to Anthony Richardson. Might the Colts face a QB controversy for their next game?

Guess not. Not 18 hours after the final whistle in Houston, the Colts announced they cut Daniel Jones. The same QB who led them to an 8-2 start last season and whom was signed to a 2-year/$88M contract this past offseason. The same QB who the Colts did not want to ship to Minnesota or Baltimore before last week’s trade deadline, who would have offered some draft compensation. Granted, the Colts’ season is the road to nowhere, but this sort of move only amplifies the missteps the planning of the franchise. They do save some cap space, but this only amplifies matters.

THE CRITICAL PLAY:

3:54, 1nd Quarter, 2nd and 10, IND Ball @ the HOU 38; Daniel Jones pass intended for TE Tyler Warren incomplete (pass defended by LB Jake Hansen).

At this point in the game, the Colts led the Texans 3-0 and had just ended up with a rather silly but effective interception. Mainly on the strength of a 26-yard pass play from Jones to Quez Watkins, the Colts were again in scoring position in HOU territory. After a short incompletion on 1st and 10, Jones was again in a shotgun set, taking the snap. TE Warren, the Colts most dangerous receiver at this point, lined up on the offensive right side and was running an in-breaking route that would have netted at least a Colts’ first down closer to the Houston red zone. However, the LB in coverage, Hansen, read the play and got his hand out to deflect the pass. This allowed Houston to force the Colts into an obvious pass play. After another incompletion, the Colts settled for a long FG, which they missed. Houston then scored on three of the next four possessions to take complete control of the game.

Had the Colts made that completion, maybe they only go up 6-0, but they would have taken greater control. Houston, already under immense pressure from the implosion in Cleveland, might have pressed too much, leading to even more mistakes. Likely this Colts’ team wasn’t winning on Thursday but had Jones thrown that pass to where Warren could get it for a good completion, momentum might have favored the Colts even more. For Houston, a team that seems to produce more bad luck for itself than good, they got some good fortune for once.

FUN WITH NUMBERS:

3: Stroud’s consecutive game streak for a number of stats: CJ Stroud’s done all of the following over the past three games:

  • Thrown an INT (bad)
  • Sacked just once a game (good)
  • Thrown for at least 3 TDs (uh, actually, really, really good)

Now, if Stroud and the Texans could spin that into at least a 3-game or greater win streak…that would be even more helpful.

4813: Days since the Houston Texans last won a game at “Reliant Stadium”. This stat has the caveat that after 2013, the Texans renamed Reliant to NRG. However, this past offseason, the Texans switched it back to Reliant. The last win at Reliant when it was Reliant: Sept 15, 2013, when the Texans came back to beat the Titans 30-24. This also snapped an 11-game losing streak at “Reliant”, as Houston lost the remaining 7 games in 2013 as well as the 1st 4 of the new “Reliant” era in 2026.

GAME BALLS:

RB David Montgomery: Since his 60 yard/2 TD rushing performance in Week 1, he’s only rushed for 78 yards and no TDs. This game was his first since Week 5. 26 carries for 107 yards (season highs for any Texans back in a game) and 3 receptions for 17 yards did quite nicely. How invaluable would this have been against the Browns in the second half? With a potentially treacherous road slate coming up, if Montgomery can run like this, Houston may yet have reason for hope.

DE Will Anderson, Jr.: 5 Tackles/2 Solo/1 sack/2 TFLs/4 QB Hits/1 safety. Even without Danielle Hunter, Anderson almost single-handedly destroyed the Colts’ offense.

RG Ed Ingram/RT Braden Smith: Maybe it was only a Colts’ squad playing out the string but consider: 83 of the Texans’ season-high 167 yards rushing came going to the offensive right, with the average rush going for over 5 yards/play. While a couple of the plays had Blake Fisher in as the extra blocker, the right side of the line was mainly Ingram and Smith. With winter coming, keeping up that high standard of play is a must.

DE Chris Braswell: Gets elevated from the practice squad to the active roster with a chance to make something happen for a team that could use the help, and he gets injured on the opening kickoff. It won’t make up for the injury, but we’ll ship a game ball his way.

SHOULD BE FORCED TO LISTEN TO CARLIE IRSAY-JORDAN’S GAME-DAY AUDIO AND HANDWRITE ON FANCY STATIONARY THE FULL TRANSCRIPT AFTER OVEREATING STALE TACO CABANA NACHOS:

Houston’s Kickoff Coverage: Not everything was perfect in this game for the Texans. For the Texans, they did manage to give up a lot of yards on kickoff returns. Even on the opening kickoff, which could have been downed for a touchback to the IND 35, Colts RB/KR Seth McGowan ran it back for 40 yards, giving the Colts the ball in prime field position, allowing them to get that opening FG. McGowan gashed Houston for 117 yards on 3 kickoff returns. That put a lot of pressure on a mercurial defense. However, the defense did respond. Once McGowan left due to injury, the numbers worked out a little better, but this season has not been the best on the coverage front.

Colts PK Spencer Shrader: A TDATDA Game Ball winner the last time these two met, it was the complete opposite this time. 1-of-3 on FGs, including a momentum-killing hook of a makable 56-yarder in the 1st quarter.  

With this win, Houston moves to 4-6, alone in second place in the AFC South and two games (effectively three) games back of the 7-seed Browns in the AFC. Houston gets an extended break before a defacto playoff game next Sunday against the struggling Ravens at Reliant. Kickoff slated for noon CST and can be seen on CBS/Paramount+

In a Friday appearance on the “Wolf & Luke Show,” general manager Monti Ossenfort said Beck suffered back spasms about halfway through Thursday’s practice. The Cardinals limited Beck the rest of the session and held him out of Friday’s workout. Ossenfort did not see this as a long-term issue.

“I don’t think so,” he said. “We’re just concerned right now here with the next 24 to 48 hours. We’re giving Josh the reps and getting him ready to play. Carson dealt with this a little bit earlier in the season, and in his role at the time, we were very safe with what we asked him to do and took our time with it. We’ll see how it goes here.”

NFL Makes Announcement on Chiefs Rookie Emmett Johnson | Yahoo! Sports

The NFL announced that Emmett Johnson has won its weekly honor. The league also uploaded a video of his Week 10 highlights on Instagram.

@emmettj_ is the Week 10 @pepsi Rookie of the Week

Johnson has outplayed his draft status and making a name for himself as a rising star. Kansas City will continue to rely on him as the season progresses, especially with his ability to contribute as a running back and receiver.

Injuries to Drake Maye and Puka Nacua Lighten the Challenge of the Chiefs’ Upcoming Gauntlet | Sports Illustrated

Without Maye, New England’s offense is led by backup quarterback Tommy DeVito—an obvious downgrade for the 5-5 Patriots.

Meanwhile, Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua certainly won’t be on the field against the Chiefs in Los Angeles one week after Thanksgiving due to an injury and suspension. Without getting into the details of the (injury/suspension) designation, the already-injury-riddled Rams will be missing at least one key weapon when they host KC.

Veteran receiver Davante Adams could potentially return in time to face the Chiefs, but that’s far from a certainty. On the defensive side of the ball, former Chiefs cornerback Jaylen Watson has been ruled out for the rest of the year due to a shoulder injury.

Recalling some great moments in Arrowhead Stadium history as Chiefs prep for move | The Kansas City Star

Some top moments since the venue opened in 1972:

The most unforgettable game in Arrowhead history came on Jan. 23, 2022, when Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes hit Travis Kelce for an 8-yard overtime touchdown to beat the Buffalo Bills 42-36 in the AFC Divisional Round — a finish that later won an ESPY as ESPN’s “Game of the Year.”

The venerable stadium just east of downtown also set a Guinness World Record in 2014, when crowd noise hit 142.2 decibels during the Chiefs’ “Monday Night Football” rout of the New England Patriots.

Chiefs’ Trey Smith helps distribute 400 Thanksgiving meals to Kansas City families | KMBC 9

Five players who are not working

L’Jarius Sneed, CB, Chiefs

How he got there: Signed a one-year, $1.2 million contract (up to $5 million in incentives)
2026 stat to know: 128.3% coverage DVOA (not enough snaps to qualify but higher is worse)
Comparable 2025 stat: 10.8% coverage DVOA

The Chiefs turned over almost their entire secondary this offseason and have gotten a lot of value out of second-year corner Nohl Williams and first-round rookie Mansoor Delane. But they brought back Sneed, a key player on their back-to-back Super Bowl-winning teams in 2022 and 2023, to play in the slot. That hasn’t worked out as well.

Around the NFL

Colts waive QB Daniel Jones in puzzling cap move, turn to Anthony Richardson in Week 12 | The Athletic

Jones, 29, has struggled all season, throwing 13 interceptions to just seven touchdowns in 11 games while completing a career-low 58.4 percent of his passes. The Colts (3-8) have lost six of their past seven games. Their decision to cut Jones now will result in a $35.2 million dead cap hit for the 2027 season — a figure that could have been significantly reduced had the Colts simply benched him and waited to cut him in March.

Patriots WR A.J. Brown expected to miss multiple weeks due to hamstring injury, per report | CBS Sports

Brown suffered the hamstring injury during their Week 10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Germany. The 29-year-old has dealt with numerous injuries this season, finding himself on the injury report more times than not.

The three-time Pro Bowler suffered an ankle injury in their season opener and was placed on injured reserve, missing four games. After he returned, he then missed two games due to a knee strain.

NFL will consider requiring minimum-night stays for international games | Pro Football Talk

“Currently, we leave those football decisions on when the team arrives in the market to the club,” NFL executive V.P. of club business, major events, and international Peter O’Reilly told The Athletic. “It is something that we’ll consider moving forward on: Do we put some minimum nights in a market in there? It’s something we’ll look at.”

The league already does it for the Super Bowl, mandating a full-week experience that includes multiple press conferences, the annual “Opening Night” media extravaganza, and practicing at designated facilities.

In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride

Have the Chiefs finally fixed their pass rush?

Brandon Thorn of Establish the Run is as respected as any offensive line analyst covering the game, and he currently has the Jets ranked as his 12th-best offensive line in the league. He has the Falcons at 19th. Not world beaters, but this wasn’t the Chiefs taking advantage of the early-season Packers MASH unit offensive line.

This weekend should set up well for another dominant performance by the Chiefs’ D-Line. The Cardinals’ quarterbacks have been sacked 8 times over the past two weeks. Thorn ranks their offensive line as the third worst in the league. This could be yet another get-right game for the defensive side of the ball before things start to get real.

item.title: NFL didn't know Puka Nacua had surgery when agreeing to suspension
item.description: The sudden decision of the NFL to suspend receiver Puka Nacua three games raises plenty of relevant questions.
item.content:encoded:
The sudden decision of the NFL to suspend receiver Puka Nacua three games raises plenty of relevant questions. On Friday, a technically irrelevant question was answered.

After Rams coach Sean McVay disclosed to reporters that Nacua had surgery to repair a torn MCL suffered during a Week 9 win over the Commanders, Judy Battista of NFL Network reported this: "The NFL did not know Puka Nacua had had knee surgery on Tuesday when it suspended him yesterday."

Surely, that's accurate; Judy is a solid reporter. But that extra fact doesn't matter to the NFL's ultimate handling of Nacua.

The report creates the impression that, during the negotiations that resulted in the three-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy, Nacua and/or his representatives withheld material information. That, at some level, the league had been duped by the lack of knowledge that Nacua had undergone surgery that will sideline him for "a couple months."

First, the suspension (as the league affirmatively explained on Thursday) is separate from the injury. The NFL listed multiple examples of players who served suspensions while injured.

Second, whether Nacua (who had already missed one of the four minimum games he's required to miss while on IR), was already going to serve the entirety of the suspension while on injured reserve with or without surgery.

Third, the surgery and the extended absence actually avoids the possibility that Nacua would have returned to action exactly one game after finishing his suspension, resulting in no net games missed due to the suspension.

The mere existence of the report represents an implicit acknowledgement by the league that the negotiated suspension, aimed at allowing Nacua to double-dip when it comes to his stint on injured reserve and his suspension, underscores the broader question of whether players should be allowed to serve a suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy when otherwise unable to play. That's a separate issue for the NFL to revisit, if it chooses, through a potential revision to the terms of the policy.

As explained on Friday, the league could have refused the deal. It could have insisted on pushing the issue through the full process, with Judge Sue L. Robinson conducting a hearing and the outcome potentially being appealed (by Nacua and/or the league) to the Commissioner. But that would have entailed a non-zero-percent chance that Nacua wouldn't have been suspended at all.

For Nacua, the goal was to get the suspension served while injured. The fact that he had surgery before the agreement was reached gave him more of a buffer than the NFL knew about, expanding the window during which the suspension could be fully served before the end of the 2026 season without Nacua missing time due to the suspension. Which would still allow Nacua to have this issue behind him before the 2027 offseason, when he signs a new contract with the Rams, has the franchise tag applied, or becomes a free agent.

Of course, Nacua now needs to tread lightly. The league has made it clear that "any further violation of the Personal Conduct Policy, including failing to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program, will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the League." To the extent that the league isn't thrilled by the perception/reality that it allowed Nacua to serve his suspension at a time when he otherwise could not play, the league could be ready to pounce on any opportunity to impose a longer suspension that would apply when Nacua is healthy again.

item.title: Philadelphia mayor wants the Eagles to play in a dome
item.description: The Eagles will become an indoor team if the mayor of Philadelphia gets her way.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles will become an indoor team if the mayor of Philadelphia gets her way.

“I want a dome,” Mayor Charelle L. Parker said on 93.3 WMMR, via the Philadelphia Inquirer. “Don’t you tell. This is a secret between us. I just saw a rendering of this beautiful dome that they’re talking about for the Bears.”

Moving into a dome would change the character of late-season and playoff games in Philadelphia, which are often affected by snow, wind and cold. Plenty of fans won't like it. But politicians and NFL owners often prefer stadiums with roofs because they bring in lucrative events, indoor sports, concerts, conventions and trade shows.

The Eagles told season ticket holders last year that they are looking at either renovations to Lincoln Financial Field or a new stadium. Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie has committed only to staying in "the region," not in the city of Philadelphia, but both Parker and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro have said they want the Eagles to remain in the city.

The Eagles' lease at Lincoln Financial Field runs through the 2032 season.

item.title: Sean Payton gives curious answer on Broncos’ vision for Jahdae Barron

item.content:encoded:
With the recent extension of cornerback Riley Moss and the desire for the Denver Broncos to revisit contract negotiations with Ja’Quan McMillian, many fans across Broncos Country have wondered what the vision is for second-year cornerback Jahdae Barron.

The Broncos have locked up both their boundary corners long-term in Moss and Patrick Surtain II. Knowing that, it’s a given that Barron isn’t going to see any significant reps on the outside in the near future unless an injury were to occur. If McMillian departs in free agency after this season, kicking him inside to the nickel spot to replace Ja’Quan makes a lot of sense. Though that’s a bridge the team will have to wait and cross in due time.

Yesterday after practice, Head Coach Sean Payton was asked how Barron fit in with the defense. I thought Payton gave a curious answer. Your mileage may vary, but this is what he had to say on the issue.

“It’s all year-to-year. In other words, relative to Jahdae, he’s got that flexibility to play in the dime stuff, play outside,” stated Payton.

With Denver’s cornerbacks now healthy, it seems likely, based off the aforementioned, that Barron’s only chance of seeing the field this year [barring injury] is going to be in Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph’s dime packages. That’s not necessarily the news Broncos Country wants to hear, with many of them longing for the 2025 first-round pick to have a larger role in the defense.

Moving forward, as noted, things do remain fluid. On multiple occasions, Payton and Joseph have touted Barron’s outside and inside flexibility. One thought that has rolled through my mind, as well as many of yours, is whether or not Jahdae could have a future at the safety position—potentially replacing Brandon Jones, who is a free agent at the end of this season.

Back when Payton was coaching the New Orleans Saints, they drafted Ohio State standout Malcolm Jenkins in the first round of the 2009 NFL Draft. Like Barron, Jenkins was also a Jim Thorpe Award winner. During his rookie season, he spent time on the boundary but had most of his snaps inside at the nickel in Gregg Williams’ defense.

The following year, he would move to free safety, a position he would man for the Saints and Philadelphia Eagles for the next twelve years of his career. Asked as a follow up to the first question, Payton gave his answer on Barron’s ability to play safety. He kept it short and sweet.

“That’s not something we’ve thought about or discussed.”

All things considered, I am a bit surprised by Payton’s answer. Though the fluidity with the year-to-year comment does make a bit of sense. Given Barron’s versatility and ability to play multiple roles, he’s a good player to have in the defense. But the commentary given by Payton makes it a little ambiguous as to what the future has in store for Barron.

For now, apparently Barron will be relegated to dime package looks. Beyond this season? That’ll be determined with whatever moves they make in the offseason.

What do you think, Broncos Country? Give me your thoughts on Payton’s comments and where you see Barron fitting in with the team moving forward.
